questions.short_title: Internet of Things in the Maritime Industry
questions.text_verbatim: Maritime industries have taken several initiatives to explore new digital technologies and "Internet of things (loT)" is one of such initiatives. With brief introduction on the principles of loT, explain the following. a) Advantages and Disadvantages of using loT in maritime industry. (6) b) How loT is changing the maritime industry. (5) c) How loT is used in Energy Efficiency optimization and predictive Maintenance. (5)

subparts.text: Advantages and disadvantages of using IoT in the maritime industry.
How IoT is changing the maritime industry.
How IoT is used in energy efficiency optimisation and predictive maintenance.

blocks.p: The Internet of Things is the connection of physical equipment - machinery, sensors, instruments - to a network, so that it can report its own condition and, in some cases, be acted upon remotely. The architecture is a chain of four stages:

ul: Sense. Equipment is fitted with sensors and given a network address - temperature, pressure, vibration, flow, torque, position.
Connect. A shipboard network gathers the data, with edge processing on board to filter, compress and act on time-critical items locally; the rest goes ashore over the satellite link.
Analyse. A shore platform stores and aggregates the data, comparing a machine against its own history and against sister ships across the fleet.
Act. The analysis produces a decision - clean the hull, change the bearing, alter the trim - and that decision is fed back to the ship.

blocks.p: The essential change is not the sensor. Ships have always been instrumented. It is that the reading no longer dies where it is taken.

blocks.h: 2. a) Advantages in the maritime industry

ul: Continuous condition monitoring in place of periodic manual readings, so a trend is visible long before a limit is reached.
Measured energy performance. Fuel is the largest operating cost, and waste that cannot be measured cannot be managed.
Early warning of developing faults, reducing unplanned breakdown, off-hire and the cost of consequential damage.
Remote diagnostics and shore support - specialist and maker assistance available to the ship without waiting for attendance.
Automated reporting for statutory and commercial purposes, removing manual transcription and its errors.
Cargo monitoring, particularly reefer containers and temperature- or atmosphere-sensitive cargo, with alarms before the cargo is lost.
Better commercial and technical decisions - spares holding, drydock scope, chartering and voyage planning all improve when they rest on measured data.

Cyber risk is the dominant disadvantage. Every connection enlarges the attack surface, and connecting operational technology - engine controls, steering, ballast, cargo systems - to information technology networks exposes control systems that were previously safe because they were isolated.
Bandwidth dependence. Satellite communication is limited, costly and can be lost, and a system designed around constant connectivity degrades when it is not there.
Cost and integration. High capital outlay, and real difficulty retrofitting sensors and data buses to legacy machinery never designed to report anything.
Data quality. An uncalibrated or drifting sensor produces confident nonsense, and a prediction built on it is worse than no prediction at all.
Data overload and alarm fatigue where outputs are not filtered to what actually needs a decision.
Skills. A real competence gap both on board and ashore, and the opposite danger of de-skilling - an engineer who trusts the display and stops using his senses.
Data ownership and vendor lock-in. Who owns the ship's data - owner, charterer or the platform supplier - and proprietary formats that make changing supplier expensive.
Liability. Responsibility when a predictive system fails to predict, or advises a wrong intervention, is not settled.

blocks.h: 4. b) How IoT is changing the maritime industry

blocks.p: The change is structural rather than merely technical:

ul: Maintenance philosophy. The industry is moving from calendar-based overhaul to condition-based and predictive maintenance - work done because the machine needs it, not because the date arrived.
Where technical management happens. Fleet operations centres ashore now monitor machinery continuously, so decisions that were the chief engineer's alone are increasingly shared with a shore team.
Commercial transparency. Ship performance is measurable, so speed and consumption warranties, performance claims and charter-party disputes rest on data rather than on assertion.
Survey and class. Remote survey and remote support reduce the need for physical attendance, and classification societies accept approved condition-monitoring arrangements.
Digital twins. A modelled counterpart of the real machinery allows an intervention to be simulated before it is made.
The wider supply chain. Voyage and port-call optimisation, including just-in-time arrival, depends on ships and ports exchanging data.
Autonomy. IoT is the enabling layer beneath autonomous and smart-ship development - there is no remote or autonomous operation without it.
Regulatory administrability. The energy-efficiency regime that came into force in January 2023 requires continuous data collection, and digitalisation is what makes that practical.

blocks.p: This limb has become commercially compulsory rather than optional. EEXI and the operational carbon intensity indicator (CII) have applied since 1 January 2023, and the EU Emissions Trading System was extended to maritime transport from 1 January 2024 - so at the date of this paper, fuel burned has a direct regulatory and financial consequence. IoT is how that is managed:

ul: Hull and propeller performance is monitored as a trend against a baseline, so fouling is quantified. Hull cleaning and propeller polishing are then done on evidence rather than on a fixed interval - too early wastes money, too late wastes fuel.
Trim optimisation - measuring actual power required at various trims and draughts and running at the best one.
Engine performance monitoring - shaft power and torque meters, cylinder pressures and exhaust temperatures compared with the shop trial baseline, so deterioration and maladjustment are found early.
Weather routing and speed optimisation using live and forecast data, including slow steaming and just-in-time arrival instead of steaming hard to wait at anchor.
Auxiliary and boiler load management, cutting unnecessary running machinery, and using shore power where it is available.
Automated data collection for the mandatory fuel-consumption reporting and rating regimes, removing manual error from a calculation that now has consequences.

blocks.p: Maintenance can be placed on a ladder: breakdown, then planned or calendar, then condition-based, then predictive. IoT is what makes the last two possible at scale.

ul: What is measured - vibration signature, bearing and winding temperature, pressures and differential pressures, thermography, lubricating-oil condition and wear debris, and overall performance efficiency.

How it works - each parameter is trended against an established baseline; the analysis identifies a developing fault by its signature, and the model estimates the remaining useful life so the work can be planned into a convenient port or drydock.

Why it matters - components are changed when they need changing, so there is less unnecessary opening-up of healthy machinery, fewer unplanned failures, lower spares holding, less off-hire, and better use of the crew's time.

Class recognition - classification societies already permit approved condition-monitoring and planned-maintenance schemes to stand in place of opening up machinery for survey, which converts the technical benefit into a survey and cost benefit.

blocks.h: 7. What has to be in place for it to work

blocks.p: Three conditions are worth stating because they are where these projects fail. First, cyber risk management is mandatory, not optional: resolution MSC.428(98) requires cyber risks to be appropriately addressed in the safety management system, and the IMO's guidelines on maritime cyber risk management, in the revision current at this date, set out the approach - identify, protect, detect, respond, recover. Second, the data must be trustworthy: calibrated sensors, an established baseline, and enough bandwidth to move what matters. Third, people - trained crew and shore staff, a clear agreement on who owns the data and who acts on it, and an engineer who retains the judgement and the confidence to overrule the system when his own senses tell him something different.

The marks are 6 + 5 + 5 with an unmarked introduction, and the answer is built to that. The introduction is genuinely brief - four bullets - because it earns nothing directly and every line spent there is taken from a marked limb.

Limb (a) is split into two separate steps, advantages and disadvantages, and that is deliberate. It is the six-mark limb, it explicitly asks for both, and the commonest failure is an enthusiastic page on benefits followed by two thin lines of drawbacks. Separating them forces the balance and makes it visible to the examiner.

Limb (b) is not the same question as limb (a). 'How IoT is changing the industry' asks about a structural shift - where maintenance decisions are taken, where technical management sits, how ships are surveyed and chartered - not about what one sensor does on one ship. Answering (b) with more advantages is the most common way to waste five marks here.

blocks.h: This is legitimately an engineering answer - but one limb is regulated

blocks.p: No IMO instrument requires IoT or prescribes how it is implemented. So most of this answer properly rests on engineering and management reasoning rather than on regulation, and that is not a weakness. What it does mean is that you should not invent a rule to make the answer look authoritative.

But the moment you connect the ship you engage something that IS regulated. Resolution MSC.428(98) requires cyber risks to be appropriately addressed in the safety management system, and the IMO guidelines on maritime cyber risk management give the five-function approach. Similarly the energy-efficiency limb has hard anchors - EEXI and CII in force from 1 January 2023, and EU ETS applying to shipping from 1 January 2024. Put the regulation where it genuinely belongs, in the risks and in the energy limb, and the answer reads like an engineer's rather than a brochure's.
Digitalisation is the fastest-moving topic on any of these papers, so anything you read about it describes a much later state of the art. Two boundaries matter for a paper of this date.

First, the IMO's guidelines on maritime cyber risk management were revised again after this sitting. If you cite a revision number, cite the one current at the paper's date - safest of all, cite MSC.428(98), which is the mandatory hook and has not moved. Second, do not describe later developments in autonomous shipping or artificial intelligence as though they already existed. The energy-efficiency anchors used here - EEXI and CII from 1 January 2023, EU ETS from 1 January 2024 - were all genuinely in force at this sitting, and EU ETS by only three months, which makes it a strong and current point to raise.

ul: Unbalanced limb (a). Six marks explicitly asks for advantages AND disadvantages.
Answering (b) with more of (a). (b) is about the structural change to the industry, not about benefits to one ship.
Omitting cyber risk. It is the single most important disadvantage and it is the only part of this topic that is mandatory.
Quoting fuel savings or downtime reductions as percentages. Those figures are vendor-sourced and installation-specific. State the mechanism, not a number you cannot defend.
Treating condition-based and predictive maintenance as the same thing. Condition-based acts on the measured present state; predictive models the future state and estimates remaining useful life.
Describing IoT as new instrumentation. Ships were always instrumented; what changed is connectivity and analysis.
Forgetting that bandwidth is finite. A design that assumes constant high-rate connectivity at sea is not a marine design.

OT versus IT. Expect to be pressed on why connecting engine control systems to the ship's business network is different from connecting an office computer. The answer is that operational technology was previously safe by isolation.
'What if the sensor is wrong?' A favourite. Calibration, baseline validity and sanity-checking against independent readings are the answer - not more data.
De-skilling. An examiner may ask whether you would still walk the engine room. The expected answer is yes, and why.
Class and survey. Be ready for the link to approved condition-monitoring schemes standing in place of opening up machinery.
Who owns the data? Owner, charterer or platform provider - there is no single answer, and saying so with the reasons is stronger than picking one.
The energy link. Expect a follow-up connecting monitoring to CII, because that is what turns a nice-to-have into a commercial necessity.

blocks.p: For the principles, four words: SENSE - CONNECT - ANALYSE - ACT. For limb (a), remember that every advantage has a shadow: more data brings data quality problems; more connection brings cyber risk; more automation brings de-skilling; more shore support brings questions of ownership and liability. Pairing them that way gives you a balanced limb (a) without memorising two separate lists.
For limb (c), the two applications answer two different questions: energy efficiency asks 'am I wasting fuel right now?', predictive maintenance asks 'what is about to break?'

questions.understand_first: Strip away the marketing and the Internet of Things is one simple idea: put sensors on things that were previously silent, connect them, and let the data be acted upon somewhere other than beside the machine. A ship has always been full of instruments - the difference is that their readings used to die in a logbook. IoT means the bearing temperature that used to be written down at 0400 is now trended ashore against ten sister ships, and somebody predicts the failure before it happens. That single shift explains everything the question asks. Note also what this question is NOT: no IMO instrument requires IoT or prescribes how it is done. That means the answer is legitimately an engineering and management answer - but the moment you connect a ship you engage cyber risk, and THAT is regulated, so the regulatory content in this answer sits in the risks, not in the technology.

What makes it work is a valid established baseline and calibrated sensors - an uncalibrated sensor produces confident nonsense and a prediction built on it is worse than none.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is IoT changing the maritime industry structurally?
retrieval_cards.answer: Maintenance moves from calendar-based to condition-based and predictive; technical management moves ashore into fleet operations centres; measurable performance changes charter parties and claims; remote survey and support reduce attendance; digital twins allow simulation before intervention; voyage and port-call optimisation extends across the supply chain; and it is the enabling layer beneath autonomous shipping.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why should an engineer not simply trust the monitoring system?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because sensors drift and baselines go stale, so the system can be confidently wrong; because over-reliance de-skills the engineer; and because responsibility for a failure the system did not predict remains unsettled. The engineer must keep the judgement and the confidence to overrule the system.

blocks.h: 1. What ammonia is, and why it is proposed

blocks.p: Ammonia is NH3. The molecule contains no carbon, so its combustion produces no carbon dioxide at the point of use, and because it contains no sulphur it produces no SOx and no fuel-borne particulates. That single property is the whole reason it is under discussion as a marine fuel.

It has two further practical advantages over hydrogen, which is the other carbon-free candidate. It liquefies readily - either by modest refrigeration or by modest pressure - so it does not demand cryogenic storage near absolute zero. And it is already manufactured, stored, shipped and handled worldwide in very large quantities as a fertiliser feedstock, so an industrial base, a seaborne trade and a body of handling experience already exist. Ammonia may itself be regarded as a practical hydrogen carrier.

The central technical difficulty is energy density. Ammonia carries less than half the energy of fuel oil per tonne, and because liquid ammonia is also less dense in energy terms per unit volume, a ship needs roughly two and a half to three times the tank volume to carry the same energy. On a fixed hull that volume is taken from cargo, ballast or accommodation.

It is stored as a liquid, either fully refrigerated at about minus 33 degrees Celsius at atmospheric pressure, or pressurised at ambient temperature, or by a semi-refrigerated combination - the same three options familiar from gas carrier practice.

Ammonia is also a poor fuel to burn. It has a narrow flammability range, a high ignition energy, a high autoignition temperature and a very slow flame speed. It will not reliably compression-ignite on its own, so a marine two-stroke burns it in dual-fuel mode with a pilot fuel - which means a conventional fuel system, and a residual carbon emission, remain on board. Materials must also be selected with care: ammonia attacks copper, brass, zinc and some alloys, so conventional pipework, gauges and instrument fittings cannot simply be reused.

blocks.h: 3. Safety, and the regulatory route at this sitting

blocks.p: Ammonia reverses the usual hazard priority. With LNG the dominant hazard is flammability; with ammonia it is acute toxicity. It is harmful, and then rapidly fatal, at concentrations far below those at which it would burn, so a release that presents no fire risk at all may still be lethal. It is corrosive to the eyes and the respiratory tract, and although it has a strong warning odour, that odour cannot be relied upon at dangerous concentrations.

Design therefore concentrates on containment and separation: double-walled fuel piping with the annular space monitored, fuel-preparation machinery in gas-tight enclosures with dedicated extraction, extensive gas detection, water deluge and absorption arrangements, controlled release and venting, and protected escape routes and safe-refuge arrangements for the crew.

The regulatory position at the date of this paper is the key point and it is one of absence. There was no IMO instrument in force governing the use of ammonia as a marine fuel. The IGF Code is the mandatory code for low-flashpoint fuels, but its detailed prescriptive provisions covered natural gas only. Where a fuel is not prescribed by the Code, the ship is approved through the alternative design and arrangements route of SOLAS regulation II-1/55, in which equivalence to the Code's goal and functional requirements is demonstrated by risk assessment and approved by the Administration or a recognized organization acting for it. In practice the technical detail was carried by classification-society rules. IMO work was under way but unfinished: the sub-committee on carriage of cargoes and containers had agreed fundamental principles to account for the toxicity of the fuel at its session of 20 to 29 September 2023, with the draft interim guidelines still to be finalised. Do not write that interim guidelines were in place.

There is no established bunkering infrastructure for ammonia as a fuel. Ammonia terminals exist for the chemical trade, but bunkering a ship is a different operation and is not widely available. It cannot be an open transfer: it requires closed, vapour-returned, leak-monitored connections with emergency release couplings, and a controlled exclusion zone.

Crew competence is a genuine gap. The STCW training regime for low-flashpoint fuels was framed around gas, and toxic-fuel operation demands additional training, different personal protective equipment, respiratory protection, dedicated medical first-aid and antidote arrangements, and rehearsed rescue from an enclosed space filled with a toxic vapour rather than an asphyxiant one. Purging, inerting and gas-freeing become routine engineering operations rather than occasional ones.

Two costs dominate. First, the fuel. Almost all ammonia produced today is grey - made from natural gas by steam reforming and the Haber-Bosch process - so it is carbon-intensive upstream even though it is carbon-free at the funnel. Green ammonia, made from renewable hydrogen, is what the sustainability claim actually depends on, and it is scarce and considerably more expensive. Second, the ship: larger tanks, double-walled systems, gas-tight enclosures and safety systems raise the capital cost, and the space they occupy is a permanent loss of earning capacity.

The commercial case therefore does not rest on fuel price - on that basis ammonia loses. It rests on regulation putting a price on carbon and on charterers valuing a low-carbon voyage. At the date of this paper that pressure was real and increasing: the EU Emissions Trading System was extended to maritime transport from 1 January 2024, and the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, adopted in July 2023, set the direction for the sector. Ammonia is best judged as a long-term candidate whose economics are created by regulation.

Carbon-free at the funnel is not the same as sustainable overall, and a good answer says so. Three qualifications matter. The production pathway decides whether any real carbon saving occurs at all. Combustion produces nitrous oxide (N2O), a greenhouse gas hundreds of times more potent than CO2, so even a small quantity can erode the benefit; and NOx control is still required. And unburnt ammonia slip is both a toxic hazard and an environmental one, requiring after-treatment. The environmental gain is real, but it is conditional on green production and on effective exhaust after-treatment, not automatic.

Ammonia is technically feasible - the engines and the containment can be built, and orders had been placed by the date of this paper - but it is not yet mature. The binding constraints are not the engine; they are safety engineering, crew competence, bunkering supply and the availability of green ammonia, with the regulatory framework still being written at this sitting. It is best described as a credible long-term candidate for deep-sea decarbonisation whose viability is conditional - on green production, on infrastructure, and on a carbon price - rather than as a fuel ready for general adoption.

The stem names four viability tests - technical, operational, safety and commercial. They are the mark scheme. Steps 2 to 5 answer them one at a time and in the stem's own words, so the examiner can tick each. The commonest way to lose marks here is to write a long, enthusiastic essay about ammonia in general that answers two of the four well and never mentions the other two.

Step 1 and step 7 are cheap and valuable: a short factual opening establishes that you know what the fuel is, and a reasoned conclusion answers the word discuss. A discussion question with no verdict is incomplete however good the middle is.

blocks.h: The date of this paper - what applied and what did not

blocks.p: This is the highest-risk point on the whole paper. At the date of this examination there was no IMO instrument governing ammonia as a marine fuel. The IGF Code's detailed provisions covered natural gas only, and an ammonia-fuelled ship was approved through SOLAS II-1/55 alternative design and arrangements with class rules and a risk assessment carrying the detail. IMO work was live but unfinished - fundamental principles on toxicity had been agreed at the September 2023 session of the carriage of cargoes and containers sub-committee, and the interim guidelines were not yet finalised.

If you revise this topic from current material you will find a set of IMO interim guidelines for ships using ammonia as fuel. They post-date this paper. Writing them into this answer is a factual error about the state of the law at the sitting, and it is the single easiest way to be wrong here while sounding well informed. The same applies to anything decided at IMO sessions later in 2024.

blocks.h: The one idea that organises the whole question

blocks.p: Ammonia inverts the hazard you are trained for. Every low-flashpoint fuel course, and the whole shape of the IGF Code, is built around flammability - keep it away from ignition sources, contain the gas, ventilate the space. Ammonia is a poor fuel and a serious poison. It barely burns, and it kills at concentrations far below the flammable range. Once you see that, the rest of the answer follows: the pilot fuel follows from poor combustion, the double-walled piping and citadel follow from toxicity, the training gap follows from both, and the regulatory vacuum follows from the fact that the existing code was written for the opposite hazard.

ul: Writing the IMO interim guidelines for ammonia as fuel into this sitting. They did not exist in April 2024. This is the trap the question is built on.
Confusing ammonia as cargo with ammonia as fuel. Carriage of ammonia is long settled under the IGC Code. Its use as fuel was not. Do not merge them.
Claiming ammonia is zero-emission or zero-carbon without qualification. It is carbon-free at the point of combustion; well-to-wake it depends entirely on how the ammonia was made.
Forgetting N2O and ammonia slip. An answer that presents combustion as clean has missed the most interesting environmental point in the topic.
Treating it as a pure ammonia engine. In a compression-ignition engine it needs a pilot fuel, so it is dual-fuel.
Answering only two or three of the four named viability lenses.
Quoting specific fuel prices, efficiency percentages or newbuilding costs. These change constantly and are not verifiable; state the direction, not a figure.
The word 'sustainable' in the stem. It is an assumption, not a finding. The strong answer tests it rather than repeating it, and distinguishes green from grey ammonia.
'Future maritime applications'. The tense invites you to describe a state of affairs that has not arrived. Be accurate about what exists now and what does not.
Toxicity versus flammability. An examiner will probe whether you have understood that the dominant hazard is not the one the IGF Code was designed around.
Energy density. Expect to be asked what that means for the ship - it means lost cargo space or reduced range, which is a commercial consequence, not just a technical one.
The comparison with methanol and LNG. A short comparative sentence shows judgement; an unprompted three-page comparison shows you are answering a different question.

OPERATIONAL - there is nowhere to get it and nobody trained. SAFETY - it is a poison, not a fire. COMMERCIAL - only a carbon price makes it pay. Then finish with the honest environmental qualification: green or grey decides everything.

questions.understand_first: Ammonia interests shipping for one reason: the molecule NH3 contains no carbon, so burning it releases no CO2 at the funnel. It carries less than half the energy of fuel oil per tonne, it will not burn readily on its own, and it is acutely toxic in concentrations far below those at which you would smell danger in any other fuel. So the honest way to answer this question is not to decide whether ammonia is good or bad, but to work through four separate viability tests - technical, operational, safety and commercial - and show where each one currently stands. blocks.p: A maritime lien is a privileged claim against the vessel herself rather than against any person. It is not created by agreement and it is not registered: it attaches to the ship by operation of law at the moment the claim arises, and it does so without notice to anyone. Until it is enforced it is inchoate - a right in the ship that lies dormant; it is crystallised by arrest and realised by forced sale. Its practical significance is its rank: a maritime lien takes priority over a registered mortgage, even one registered earlier and for a far larger sum.
That combination - secret, unregistered, automatic and senior - is what distinguishes it from an ordinary possessory lien, which depends on holding the goods and is lost when possession is given up.

blocks.h: 2. How the lien travels with the property

blocks.p: This is the defining characteristic, and the Convention states it in one sentence. Article 8: the maritime liens follow the vessel, notwithstanding any change of ownership or of registration or of flag.

ul: The lien is attached to the res - the ship - and not to the owner, so selling the ship does not shed it.

It binds a bona fide purchaser for value without notice. A buyer may acquire a ship with unpaid crew wages or a salvage award still charged against her and have no means of discovering it from any register. This is why it is called a secret lien and why prudent buyers take indemnities and searches.
Reflagging and re-registration make no difference: the lien travels with the hull, not with the certificate.
It is defeated in only two ways - by a forced sale complying with article 12, which sweeps the ship clean of liens and encumbrances, or by lapse of time under article 9.

blocks.p: Under article 9 the article 4 liens are extinguished after one year unless, before then, the vessel has been arrested or seized and that arrest or seizure leads to a forced sale. Time runs from the claimant's discharge from the vessel for wage claims and from the moment the claim arises for the others, and it runs continuously, without suspension or interruption.

ul: An action in personam is brought against a person - the owner, charterer, manager or operator. The claimant must find that person, establish jurisdiction over them, and then enforce against whatever assets they have. If the defendant is a single-ship company with no other assets, a judgment in personam may be worth nothing.

An action in rem is brought against the ship herself, which is named as defendant. The court's jurisdiction is founded on the presence of the res within the jurisdiction, and the ship may be arrested.

blocks.p: The connection between the two limbs of this question is the point the examiner is looking for: the maritime lien is what gives the claimant a right in rem against the ship. Because the lien attaches to the vessel and follows her, the claimant can proceed against the vessel wherever she is found and whoever now owns her.

Arrest is not usually an end in itself. It is a coercive step: it either compels the provision of security - a P&I club letter of undertaking or a bank guarantee - so that the ship may trade on, or, if no security is forthcoming, it produces a fund through forced sale out of which the claims are paid. The two forms of action are not alternatives and may be pursued together.

blocks.h: 4. Which convention deals with maritime liens

blocks.p: The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993, adopted at Geneva on 6 May 1993 and in force from 5 September 2004. It is the successor to the earlier Brussels Conventions of 1926 and 1967 on the same subject, neither of which achieved wide acceptance. Its stated purpose is to improve the conditions for ship financing and the development of national merchant fleets - which explains its structure: it protects mortgagees by making mortgages recognisable and enforceable across States, and it does so by defining exhaustively the small class of claims that outrank them.
Article 4(1) secures five claims, against the owner, demise charterer, manager or operator, by a maritime lien on the vessel:

ul: (a) claims for wages and other sums due to the master, officers and other members of the vessel's complement in respect of their employment on the vessel, including costs of repatriation and social insurance contributions payable on their behalf;
(b) claims in respect of loss of life or personal injury, whether on land or on water, in direct connection with the operation of the vessel;
(c) claims for reward for the salvage of the vessel;
(d) claims for port, canal and other waterway dues and pilotage dues;
(e) claims based on tort arising out of physical loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel, other than loss of or damage to cargo, containers and passengers' effects carried on the vessel.

blocks.p: Article 4(2) removes two categories from limbs (b) and (e): damage from the carriage of oil or other hazardous or noxious substances for which compensation is payable under regimes providing strict liability and compulsory insurance, and damage from the radioactive properties of nuclear fuel, products or waste. The reasoning is that those claimants already have a dedicated fund, and there is no need to give them a lien as well.

Note what is not a maritime lien: cargo claims, and the claims of necessaries men - bunker suppliers, repairers and agents. They may be maritime claims founding an action in rem, but they carry no lien under article 4.

blocks.h: 6. How the liens rank among themselves - article 5

ul: The article 4 liens take priority over registered mortgages, "hypotheques" and charges, and no other claim takes priority over either, subject to article 12(3) and (4).
They rank in the order listed in article 4 - so wages before personal injury, before salvage, before dues, before tort.

But salvage liens jump the queue: a lien securing a claim for salvage reward takes priority over all other maritime liens which attached before the salvage operations were performed. The logic is obvious - the salvor preserved the very fund the others are claiming against.
Liens within each of (a), (b), (d) and (e) rank pari passu among themselves.
Salvage liens rank in the inverse order of time in which the claims accrued - the later salvage ranks first - each claim being deemed to accrue on the date the salvage operation terminated.

blocks.h: 7. The order of settlement after forced sale - article 12

blocks.p: A forced sale in a State Party sweeps the vessel clean: all registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges, except those assumed by the purchaser with the holders' consent, and all liens and other encumbrances of whatsoever nature, cease to attach to the vessel, provided the ship was within that State's jurisdiction and the sale complied with its law and with articles 11 and 12. The proceeds are then distributed in this order:

ul: 1. The costs and expenses of the arrest or seizure and of the subsequent sale, paid first out of the proceeds. These expressly include the costs of upkeep of the vessel and the crew, and the wages and other sums under article 4(1)(a) incurred from the time of the arrest or seizure.

2. Wreck-removal costs, where a State Party has so provided. Article 12(3) permits a State to provide that, where a stranded or sunken vessel has been removed by a public authority in the interest of safe navigation or protection of the marine environment, those removal costs are paid before all other claims secured by a maritime lien. This is optional, not automatic.
3. The article 4 maritime liens, in their article 5 order and subject to the salvage rules.

4. The right of retention of a shipbuilder or shiprepairer under article 7. Article 12(4) requires him to surrender possession to the purchaser, but entitles him to be satisfied out of the proceeds after the article 4 lienholders.
5. Registered mortgages, "hypotheques" and charges complying with article 1.
6. Other maritime liens granted under national law under article 6, which rank after both the article 4 liens and the registered mortgages.
7. The residue, if any, to the owner, and States Parties must ensure the proceeds are actually available and freely transferable.

blocks.p: The purchaser is then entitled to a certificate that the vessel is sold free of encumbrances, on production of which the registrar must delete the registered mortgages and charges and either register the vessel in the purchaser's name or issue a certificate of deregistration.

blocks.h: 8. The Indian statutory position, kept separate

blocks.p: In India the subject is governed domestically by the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 (No. 22 of 2017, assented 9 August 2017), which consolidated admiralty jurisdiction and vested it in the High Courts. Its scheme closely follows the Convention, and the differences are worth knowing:

ul: Section 9(1) lists the same five maritime liens in the same order, with two widenings: limb (c) covers salvage including special compensation, and limb (d) adds any other statutory dues related to the vessel.

Section 9(2) reproduces the travelling rule - the lien continues notwithstanding any change of ownership or of registration or of flag - and the one-year extinction, but with a proviso giving TWO years for wage claims under limb (a), running from the date the wage, repatriation cost or social insurance contribution fell due. That is more generous to seafarers than the Convention.

Section 10 sets the order of priority of maritime claims in an admiralty proceeding as: (a) claims where there is a maritime lien; (b) registered mortgages and charges of the same nature; (c) all other claims - with claims in a single category ranking equally, and salvage claims in inverse order of time.

blocks.p: (The stem asks about the convention, and the answer above is given at convention level. The Indian Act is set out separately because it is the law an Indian court would apply, and it should not be conflated with the Convention.)

The stem contains five separate demands in sixteen marks - define the lien, explain how it travels, explain in rem and in personam, name the convention, and give the order of settlement. That is roughly three marks each, so none of them deserves an essay and none may be skipped. The two that candidates most often lose are the last: they name the convention vaguely, or give a half-remembered priority list. The order of settlement is the single most concrete thing in the question and it is the easiest to prepare, so it should be written out as a numbered list, not narrated.

blocks.h: The idea that links the whole question

blocks.p: The lien and the action in rem are two halves of one mechanism. The maritime lien attaches to the ship rather than to a person; that is precisely what allows the claimant to sue the ship rather than a person. If you state that link explicitly - the lien is what gives the right in rem - the middle three demands of the question join up instead of reading as three unrelated definitions.

blocks.h: Why the lien is called secret, and why that matters commercially

blocks.p: There is no register of maritime liens. A buyer inspecting the ship's registry sees mortgages and charges but cannot see unpaid crew wages, an outstanding salvage award or a personal injury claim - and under article 8 all of those follow the vessel through a sale, a change of registry and a change of flag. So a purchaser can take delivery of a ship already encumbered by claims ranking ahead of the mortgage financing the purchase. This is why sale contracts carry indemnities and why a forced sale under article 12 is commercially valuable: it is the one transaction that delivers a genuinely clean ship, which is exactly why an arresting creditor's remedy has teeth.

blocks.h: The two salvage rules - state both

blocks.p: Salvage is the exception to almost every ranking rule in the Convention and both exceptions are examinable.

ul: Salvage jumps ahead of earlier liens. A salvage lien takes priority over all maritime liens which attached before the salvage operations were performed. The salvor preserved the fund everyone else is claiming against, so he is paid first out of it.

Salvage liens rank in inverse order of time. Where there is more than one salvage, the later ranks ahead of the earlier - each claim accruing on the date its salvage operation terminated. Every other category ranks pari passu.

blocks.h: What is NOT a maritime lien

blocks.p: A quick way to show command of article 4 is to say what it leaves out. Cargo claims are not secured by a maritime lien - article 4(1)(e) expressly excludes loss of or damage to cargo, containers and passengers' effects. Nor are the claims of necessaries men - bunker suppliers, repairers, agents and chandlers. These may still be maritime claims supporting an action in rem and an arrest, but they carry no lien and therefore rank behind registered mortgages. The distinction between a maritime claim and a maritime lien is exactly what the priority list is about.

blocks.h: The Indian dimension - and the statement to avoid

blocks.p: The examiner asks about the convention, so answer at convention level. The Indian statute is the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, and giving it separately is a strength: its section 9 reproduces the five liens and their order, and its section 10 gives the three-tier priority - liens, then registered mortgages, then all other claims.

Two genuine Indian divergences are worth knowing. Section 9(1)(c) covers salvage including special compensation, and section 9(1)(d) adds any other statutory dues related to the vessel. Most importantly, section 9(2) gives seafarers two years for wage claims where the Convention gives one - more generous than the Convention.

What to avoid: do not assert whether or not India is a party to the 1993 Convention. It is not necessary to answer any part of this question, and a confident statement either way is a risk for no reward. Say what the Convention provides, say what the Indian Act provides, and let the two stand side by side.

ul: Confusing a maritime claim with a maritime lien. Every lien is a claim; very few claims are liens.
Saying a maritime lien is lost on sale of the ship. It is not - article 8 is the whole point of the question's second limb.
Treating in rem and in personam as alternatives. They may be pursued together.
Putting mortgages ahead of maritime liens. Article 5 puts the liens first, which is the commercially surprising and therefore examinable point.
Forgetting that arrest and sale costs and post-arrest crew wages are paid before everything, including the liens.
Omitting the salvage inverse-order rule, or applying inverse order to all categories rather than only to salvage.
Giving a mortgage a rank ahead of the shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention. Article 12(4) puts retention after the article 4 liens but the Convention leaves mortgages behind both.

blocks.p:
"You buy a ship with a clean registry search. Can you still be caught?" Yes. Maritime liens are unregistered and follow the vessel through a change of ownership, registration and flag. Only a forced sale under article 12, or the lapse of time under article 9, clears them.

"Crew wages or the bank - who is paid first?" Crew. Article 4(1)(a) is the first maritime lien and article 5(1) puts all article 4 liens ahead of registered mortgages. And the wages incurred after arrest are paid even before that, as part of the article 12(2) costs.

"Two salvage services, one in January and one in June. Who ranks first?" June - salvage liens rank in inverse order of time.

"Is a bunker supplier's claim a maritime lien under the Convention?" No. It may be a maritime claim founding an action in rem, but article 4 does not secure it, so it ranks behind registered mortgages.

ul: Define a maritime lien in one sentence. A privileged claim attaching to the vessel by operation of law, without registration or notice, which follows her through changes of ownership, registration and flag.
Which convention, adopted where and when? The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993, adopted at Geneva on 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004.

List the five maritime liens in order. Wages; loss of life or personal injury; salvage; port, canal and waterway dues and pilotage; tort for physical loss or damage other than to cargo, containers and passengers' effects.
How long does a maritime lien last? One year under article 9, unless arrest or seizure leading to forced sale intervenes - and two years for wage claims under the Indian Act.
What is paid first out of a forced sale? The costs of arrest, seizure and sale, including upkeep of ship and crew and post-arrest wages.
Where do mortgages rank? After the article 4 maritime liens and after a shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention.
Which Indian statute governs? The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - section 9 for liens, section 10 for priority.

questions.understand_first: Ordinary law says that if you are owed money you sue the person who owes it. Shipping cannot work that way: the debtor may be a single-ship company in a jurisdiction you will never reach, and the only asset is a ship that will sail tomorrow. So maritime law does something unusual - it lets a small class of claims attach to the SHIP itself, silently and automatically, and follow her wherever she goes and whoever buys her. That is a maritime lien, and the action in rem is simply the procedure for enforcing it: you sue the ship. Everything else in this question - the priority list, the arrest, the forced sale - is the machinery for turning a ship into money and then deciding who gets paid out of it, in what order.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the maritime lien question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What a maritime lien is. 2 How it travels with the property. 3 In rem and in personam. 4 Which convention. 5 What article 4 secures. 6 How the liens rank among themselves. 7 The order of settlement after forced sale. 8 The Indian statutory position, separately.
retrieval_cards.why: Five demands in sixteen marks, so about three marks each. None deserves an essay and none may be skipped.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a maritime lien.
retrieval_cards.answer: A privileged claim against the vessel herself, attaching to her by operation of law at the moment the claim arises, without agreement, registration or notice. It is inchoate until enforced, crystallised by arrest and realised by forced sale, and it ranks ahead of registered mortgages.
retrieval_cards.why: Secret, unregistered, automatic and senior - those four words distinguish it from every ordinary lien.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a maritime lien travel with the property, and how is it ever lost?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 8 of the 1993 Convention: the maritime liens follow the vessel notwithstanding any change of ownership or of registration or of flag - so they bind even a bona fide purchaser without notice. They are lost only by a forced sale complying with article 12, which sweeps the ship clean, or by lapse of time under article 9 - one year, unless arrest or seizure leading to a forced sale intervenes.
retrieval_cards.why: The travelling rule is the second demand of the stem and the Convention answers it in a single sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish an action in rem from an action in personam, and say how the lien connects them.
retrieval_cards.answer: In personam is against a person - the owner, charterer, manager or operator - and is worth only what that person's assets are worth. In rem is against the ship herself as defendant, founded on her presence within the jurisdiction and enforced by arrest. The maritime lien is what gives the claimant the right in rem, because it attaches to the vessel and follows her. The two may be pursued together.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating the link turns three separate definitions into one mechanism, which is what the examiner is looking for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the convention and list the five claims it secures by a maritime lien.
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993 - Geneva, 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004. Article 4: (a) crew wages, repatriation and social insurance; (b) loss of life or personal injury; (c) salvage reward; (d) port, canal and waterway dues and pilotage; (e) tort for physical loss or damage, other than to cargo, containers and passengers' effects.
retrieval_cards.why: W-P-S-D-T. The order is the ranking order too, so learning the list once does two jobs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the order of settlement of claims after a forced sale under the 1993 Convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Costs and expenses of arrest or seizure and of the sale, including upkeep of vessel and crew and article 4(1)(a) wages incurred from the time of arrest. 2 Optionally, wreck-removal costs where the State has so provided under article 12(3). 3 The article 4 maritime liens in their article 5 order. 4 A shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention under article 12(4). 5 Registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges. 6 Other national maritime liens under article 6. 7 The residue to the owner.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the most concrete thing in the question and the easiest to prepare. Write it as a numbered list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Two salvage services, January and June. Which lien ranks first, and why does salvage rank oddly at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: June. Salvage liens rank in the inverse order of time in which the claims accrued, each accruing when its salvage operation terminated. Salvage also takes priority over all other maritime liens which attached before the salvage operations were performed, because the salvor preserved the very fund the other claimants are claiming against.
retrieval_cards.why: Two separate salvage rules, and inverse order applies only to salvage - not to the other categories, which rank pari passu.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is a bunker supplier's claim a maritime lien under the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Bunker suppliers, repairers, agents and other necessaries men have maritime claims which may found an action in rem and support an arrest, but article 4 does not secure them by a maritime lien, so they rank behind registered mortgages. Cargo claims are excluded in terms by article 4(1)(e).
retrieval_cards.why: Every lien is a claim; very few claims are liens. Confusing the two is the commonest error in this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the Indian Admiralty Act 2017 differ from the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 9(1) lists the same five liens in the same order, but limb (c) covers salvage including special compensation and limb (d) adds any other statutory dues related to the vessel. Section 9(2) reproduces the travelling rule and the one-year extinction but adds a proviso giving two years for wage claims - more generous to seafarers than the Convention. Section 10 gives a three-tier priority: maritime liens, then registered mortgages and charges, then all other claims, with equal ranking within a category and salvage in inverse order of time.
retrieval_cards.why: It is an Indian examination, so the domestic statute earns marks - but keep it separate from the Convention rather than merging the two.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Crew wages or the mortgagee bank - who is paid first out of a forced sale?
retrieval_cards.answer: The crew. Article 5(1) puts all article 4 maritime liens ahead of registered mortgages, and wages are the first lien in the article 4 list. Wages and upkeep incurred after the arrest rank even higher, as part of the article 12(2) costs paid first out of the proceeds.
retrieval_cards.why: It is commercially counter-intuitive that an unregistered claim beats a registered mortgage, which is exactly why it is examined.

blocks.h: 1. Where the energy to be recovered is

blocks.p: A screw propeller working behind a hull typically converts only about 65 to 72 per cent of delivered power into useful thrust. The losses are of three kinds: axial, in the sternward momentum of the race; rotational, in the swirl the blades impart to it; and frictional and vortex losses, principally the hub vortex shed from the boss. The rotational component alone is commonly of the order of 8 to 12 per cent of delivered power on a single-screw merchant ship.

The rudder is the only large body standing in that race. It is therefore both an opportunity - the swirl arrives at it already rotating, so a correctly oriented surface there sees an angle of attack for nothing - and a liability, because a plain rudder behind a bare boss adds drag and lets the hub vortex run on unchecked. The four devices below exploit the first and reduce the second.

A rudder thrust fin is a horizontal foil, usually fitted as a pair port and starboard, mounted on the rudder at or near the level of the propeller shaft, inside the slipstream. Because the race is rotating, the flow arrives at the fin with a tangential component: upward on one side of the shaft and downward on the other. Each fin is set at the angle that turns that oncoming flow into lift, and because the flow is inclined, the lift vector is tilted forward. Its horizontal component is thrust, generated with no additional power.

ul: The two fins are set at different angles, or in mirror image, because the swirl direction differs above and below the shaft.
Gains quoted in industry literature are typically of the order of 2 to 5 per cent in delivered power, and are strongly dependent on span, chord and angle of attack.
The angle is fixed at build. The device is optimised for one draught and speed and gives less, or in extreme off-design conditions nothing, elsewhere.
It is a source of added appendage drag when not loaded, and a candidate for cavitation erosion if it sits too close to the blade tips.

blocks.p: Here the recovery is built into the rudder itself rather than added to it. On a single-screw ship the propeller turns one way, so the race strikes the upper half of the rudder from one side and the lower half from the other. A conventional symmetrical rudder, aligned with the centreline, therefore meets the flow at an angle of attack of the wrong sign over half its span, producing side force, drag and early cavitation.

An asymmetric rudder cures this by making the two halves different. In the developed form - the twisted leading edge rudder - the leading edge is twisted in opposite directions above and below the shaft line, so that each half is aligned with the swirl it actually meets.

ul: The rudder becomes a swirl-recovery surface: the side force on the two halves is turned into a net forward component.
It reduces drag and cavitation, and with it rudder erosion and propeller-excited vibration.
It is handed - built for one direction of rotation - so it is a design decision, not a universal retrofit.
Because it changes the rudder body rather than adding to it, it carries no added appendage and its benefit degrades more gracefully off design than a fixed fin.

blocks.p: The propeller boss sheds a strong hub vortex, and behind a bare boss the flow separates, leaving a low-pressure wake that pulls the ship astern. A rudder bulb is a streamlined body of revolution fitted to the rudder leading edge, coaxial with the shaft and sized and positioned so that it forms an almost continuous body with the propeller hub cap, closing the gap between them.

ul: It suppresses or displaces the hub vortex, removing a pure loss.
It restores pressure behind the boss by giving the flow a body to close around instead of separating, which is a genuine reduction in resistance rather than a recovery of energy.
The diameter and the axial gap govern the result; too large or too far aft and the bulb adds more drag than it saves.
It is most often fitted together with fins, the bulb conditioning the flow the fins work in, so the two are designed as one installation and their savings are not simply additive.

blocks.p: The vane wheel, patented by Otto Grim in 1966, is the most ambitious of the four and the only one that moves. It is a freely rotating bladed wheel mounted on the shaft line immediately aft of the propeller, of larger diameter than the propeller, with no mechanical connection to it or to the shaft. It runs at its own speed, typically around a third to a half of propeller revolutions, driven entirely by the water.
Its cleverness is that one blade does two jobs at different radii:

ol: The inner portion, standing inside the propeller race, works as a turbine. It extracts energy from the swirl and axial velocity of the slipstream, and that is what drives the wheel round.

The outer portion, standing outside the race in undisturbed water, works as a propeller. Driven by the torque the inner part has extracted, it produces additional thrust over a larger disc area and therefore at higher efficiency.

blocks.p: The wheel thus takes wasted energy from a small, fast, disturbed stream and returns it as thrust in a large, slow, clean one. Gains of the order of 5 to 10 per cent were claimed and some were demonstrated. In service the device proved difficult: the long, thin, unsupported blades of the outer portion are fatigue-loaded and blade loss and shedding occurred; performance falls away in a seaway and off design, when the wheel can windmill unhelpfully; and it adds a rotating component aft of the propeller with its own bearing and clearance problems. It is now of more importance as a principle - and as an examination question - than as a device in general service.

blocks.h: 6. Whether a claimed gain is real on this ship

blocks.p: All four claims are hull-specific. A device recovers only what the propeller behind that hull actually wastes, so the gain depends on the wake field, block coefficient, propeller loading, draught and service speed. Three consequences follow, and they are where the marks are at this level. First, a quoted percentage means nothing without the condition it was measured in, and model-scale results require a scale-effect correction before they can be believed at full scale. Second, devices interact: a bulb changes the flow the fins see, so savings must be assessed for the installation as a whole. Third, the real case is the operating profile - a ship that spends its life slow-steaming at part draught will not realise a gain optimised for design condition, and the payback calculation must be built on the actual profile, on class approval of the attachment and its structure, and on the effect on manoeuvring, which a rudder-mounted device necessarily touches.

The examiner has done the structuring for you. Four devices are named and each carries 4 marks, so the answer is four equal blocks and nothing else can be substituted for them. The single most common way to lose marks here is to write a good general essay on energy-saving devices - pre-swirl stators, ducts, propeller boss cap fins, air lubrication - none of which is asked for. Answer the four printed limbs.

blocks.h: The one idea that unlocks all four

blocks.p: Rotational loss. The propeller leaves the race spinning, and that spin is energy already paid for and thrown away. Two of these devices recover it - the fin and the twisted rudder turn swirl into forward force, and the vane wheel takes it mechanically. Two stop further waste - the bulb removes the hub vortex and the separation behind the boss. If you can say which of the two categories a device is in, you can reconstruct its explanation from first principles.

blocks.h: Keep recovery and drag reduction apart

ul: Recovery - thrust fins, asymmetric and twisted rudders, vane wheels. They convert energy already in the water into thrust.
Drag and vortex reduction - rudder bulbs. They do not recover anything; they stop a loss from happening.

The bulb is often described loosely as recovering hub-vortex energy. The defensible statement is that it suppresses the vortex and restores pressure behind the boss. Say that and the point is safe either way.
Describing an asymmetric rudder as a rudder offset to one side of the centreline. The asymmetry is in the section and the twist about the shaft line, matching the opposite swirl above and below.
Saying the Grim vane wheel is geared to or driven by the shaft. It is entirely free-running; there is no mechanical connection, and that is the whole point.
Making the vane wheel the same diameter as the propeller. It is larger, and it must be, because the outer portion has to stand outside the race to act as a propeller.
Quoting a saving as a hard number. Every figure is conditional on the hull and the operating condition.
Adding the percentages of several devices together.
Ignoring manoeuvring. Anything bolted to a rudder changes the way she steers, and class will want to see the structure.

"Currently in use" in the stem. The Grim vane wheel is the odd one out - historically important, largely not in service. Say so rather than pretending it is common; an answer that quietly treats all four as current practice is weaker, not stronger.
Limb (d) is worth the same 4 marks as the others even though it is the least used. Do not short it.
The stem says the devices contribute to propulsion effectiveness, not to steering. Manoeuvring belongs in the closing judgement, not in place of the hydrodynamics.

Some of what it leaves behind is axial - water thrown astern faster than it needs to be - and some is rotational: the race leaves the disc spinning, and that spin is wasted energy. Behind the propeller of a single-screw ship sits a large flat object in exactly that spinning race: the rudder. Every device in this question does one of two things with it - it either recovers some of the rotational energy and turns it into forward thrust, or it stops wasting more, by removing a vortex or a separation the rudder itself creates. retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the rudder-efficiency question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Where the losses are - then the four printed limbs in order: (a) thrust fins, (b) asymmetric and twisted rudders, (c) rudder bulbs, (d) Grim vane wheels - then the management judgement on whether a claimed gain is real on this ship.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner prints 4 + 4 + 4 + 4. The four blocks must be equal, and the surrounding material has to be paid for out of the same 16 marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the rotational loss, and why does it matter here?
retrieval_cards.answer: The propeller leaves its race spinning as well as moving astern. That swirl is energy already paid for and thrown away - of the order of 8 to 12 per cent of delivered power on a single-screw ship. The rudder stands directly in it, which is why the rudder region is where these devices work.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single idea behind all four devices. Knowing it lets you reconstruct any of them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a rudder thrust fin produce thrust without power?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is a horizontal foil on the rudder inside the propeller race. The race is rotating, so the flow meets the fin at an angle of attack without the fin being turned. The fin develops lift, and because the oncoming flow is inclined the lift vector tilts forward; its horizontal component is thrust.
retrieval_cards.why: The mechanism is the mark. Describing the fin's shape without the inclined-lift argument earns very little.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What exactly is asymmetric about an asymmetric rudder?
retrieval_cards.answer: The section and the twist about the shaft line, not the position. The propeller race strikes the upper half of the rudder from one side and the lower half from the other, so the leading edge is twisted in opposite senses above and below the shaft to align each half with the swirl it actually meets.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest error is to describe a rudder offset to one side of the centreline. That is a different thing entirely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a rudder bulb recover energy or reduce loss?
retrieval_cards.answer: Properly, it reduces loss. It suppresses the hub vortex and gives the flow a body to close around instead of separating behind a bare boss, restoring pressure there. It is often described loosely as recovering hub-vortex energy; the safe formulation is suppression and pressure recovery.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the one device in the four that is not a recovery device, and saying so shows you understand the mechanism rather than the marketing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain how a Grim vane wheel works.
retrieval_cards.answer: It is a freely rotating wheel aft of and coaxial with the propeller, larger in diameter, with no mechanical connection to the shaft. Its inner portion stands inside the propeller race and acts as a turbine, extracting energy from the swirl and driving the wheel round; its outer portion stands outside the race in clean water and acts as a propeller, converting that energy into additional thrust over a larger disc.
retrieval_cards.why: One blade doing two jobs at two radii is the whole idea, and it is what distinguishes the vane wheel from every other device on the list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must a vane wheel be larger in diameter than the propeller?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because its outer portion has to stand outside the propeller race to work as a propeller in undisturbed water. If the wheel were the same diameter, the whole blade would sit in the slipstream and there would be no propeller portion to return the extracted energy as thrust.
retrieval_cards.why: A favourite oral follow-up, and it tests whether the turbine-plus-propeller split has actually been understood.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A maker offers a 4 per cent saving from a rudder thrust fin. What do you ask before agreeing?
retrieval_cards.answer: In what condition was the 4 per cent measured - draught, speed, loading - and was it model scale or full scale, with what scale correction? How does it behave at our actual operating profile rather than at the design point? What else is already fitted, since devices interact and savings do not simply add? What does class require for the attachment and its structure, and what is the effect on manoeuvring?
retrieval_cards.why: This is the management-level mark. Anyone can recite the mechanism; the Class I candidate interrogates the claim.

blocks.h: 1. a) The Convention - what it does and why

blocks.p: The International Convention on the Control of Harmful Anti-fouling Systems on Ships, 2001 - the AFS Convention - entered into force on 17 September 2008. Its purpose is to prohibit or restrict anti-fouling systems that are harmful to the marine environment while allowing ships to continue to control fouling.

It exists because of organotin compounds, principally tributyl tin. TBT was an outstandingly effective antifouling biocide and an outstandingly damaging pollutant: it persists, it accumulates in sediment and in the food chain, and it causes imposex and shell deformity in shellfish at concentrations of a few parts per trillion, with severe damage recorded around ports and shellfish grounds.

The Convention applies to ships entitled to fly the flag of a Party and to ships operating under a Party's authority. The substances actually controlled are listed in Annex 1, and that list can be added to by amendment - which is exactly what has since happened. Compliance is enforced through survey and certification and through inspection by port State officers, who may examine the certificate or declaration and may take a sample of the coating.
Organotin compounds acting as biocides in anti-fouling systems:

ul: no ship may apply or re-apply them - effective 1 January 2003;
from 1 January 2008 a ship must either not bear such a system, or must carry a coating that forms a barrier to it leaching from the underlying non-compliant system.

blocks.p: Cybutryne was added to Annex 1 by amendment adopted on 17 June 2021, which entered into force on 1 January 2023. It was therefore fully in force at the date of this paper, and an answer that describes only the tin position is incomplete.

ul: All ships: no application or re-application of an anti-fouling system containing cybutryne, from 1 January 2023.

Ships already bearing cybutryne in the external coating layer on that date must either remove the system or apply a coating forming a barrier to it leaching - at the next scheduled renewal of the anti-fouling system after 1 January 2023, and no later than 60 months after the last application of a cybutryne-containing system.

Limited exclusions apply, including fixed and floating platforms, FSUs and FPSOs constructed before that date which have not since been in dry dock, ships not engaged on international voyages, and ships under 400 GT on international voyages where the coastal State accepts it.

blocks.p: The practical lesson is that 'tin-free' does not mean 'unregulated'. Cybutryne was a common booster biocide in tin-free paints, so the second wave of control fell on the very coatings that replaced TBT.

blocks.h: 3. a) Documents and records to demonstrate compliance

blocks.p: What a surveyor or port State control officer will expect to be produced:

ul: International Anti-Fouling System Certificate (IAFS Certificate) - for ships of 400 gross tonnage and above engaged in international voyages, issued by or on behalf of the Administration after the required survey.

The Record of Anti-Fouling Systems - attached to and forming part of the certificate. It records the system applied, the facility that applied it and the date, and which compliance option applies to each controlled substance: never applied, applied and since removed, applied and covered with a sealer coat, or not in the external coating layer.
Declaration on Anti-Fouling System - for ships of 24 metres or more in length but less than 400 gross tonnage engaged in international voyages, signed by the owner or the owner's authorized agent.
Supporting documentation for that Declaration - a paint receipt or contractor's invoice, or equivalent evidence of what was applied.

Manufacturer's technical documentation - product data sheets and declarations confirming the composition of the system and the absence of controlled substances, together with application records: product, batch, area, dry film thickness and dates.
Survey records and reports - of the initial survey, and of any survey carried out when the anti-fouling system is changed or replaced, with the certificate endorsed or reissued accordingly.
Record of any sealer or barrier coat applied over a non-compliant system, naming the facility and the date, since that is what the certificate itself must state.
Dry-docking and planned maintenance records evidencing the last application and the next scheduled renewal - these establish the 60-month position for cybutryne.

blocks.p: One point specific to this period: since the cybutryne amendment the certificate must be in the amended model form, which carries cybutryne as well as organotins. Affected ships were given a transitional period to obtain a certificate in that form, and that transition was still running at the date of this paper.

A soluble matrix coating, traditionally rosin-based. Seawater slowly dissolves the binder, and as it dissolves it releases the biocide dispersed within it - essentially a refinement of the old soluble-matrix paints.

Because release depends on physical dissolution rather than a controlled chemical reaction, the release rate is not well regulated and tails off with time, and a thick, uneven leached layer builds up on the hull. That layer increases roughness and drag, so fuel performance degrades over the docking cycle. It is the cheapest of the four, easy to apply and easy to overcoat, and is generally suited to shorter drydock intervals and lower-activity ships.

The important difference is chemical. The biocide is chemically bonded into an acrylic copolymer backbone rather than merely mixed into a soluble binder. In seawater the surface layer hydrolyses, releasing the biocide at a controlled, near-linear rate, and the spent binder then becomes soluble and erodes away - so the coating polishes itself smooth as it works.

The consequences are a thin and stable leached layer, a predictable release rate that can be engineered to the ship's speed and activity, longer service life - commonly to a full five-year docking cycle - and better sustained hydrodynamic performance because the surface stays smooth. It costs more than CDP. Modern tin-free SPCs use copper, zinc or silyl acrylate chemistries in place of the original tin ones.
A blend of the two technologies above - rosin and copolymer chemistry combined in one binder - intended to capture some of the controlled polishing behaviour of SPC at closer to CDP cost.

The result is intermediate on every axis: more predictable release and less leached-layer build-up than pure CDP, but less precisely controlled than a true SPC; intermediate service life; intermediate price. It is a sensible compromise for moderate trading patterns and medium docking intervals. Note that 'hybrid' is a commercial label rather than a defined term, and formulations sold under it vary considerably.

These are fundamentally different: they contain no biocide at all and work by physics rather than by poisoning. A silicone or fluoropolymer elastomer gives a surface of very low surface energy and very high smoothness, to which fouling organisms cannot attach firmly. Such growth as does settle is sheared off by the water flow once the ship is moving.

Strengths: the lowest drag of any of the four, hence the best fuel performance, and no biocide released into the sea, which is the strongest environmental position. Limitations are real: performance depends on regular activity and adequate speed, so the ship fouls during prolonged idle periods or slow steaming; the film is mechanically soft and easily damaged and is difficult to repair; it requires a full tie-coat system and careful surface preparation; and it carries the highest initial cost.

The choice follows the ship's trading pattern, service speed, proportion of idle time and intended drydock interval. A fast, regularly operating ship on a five-year cycle rewards a fouling release or a good SPC; a slower ship with irregular employment and long port stays is better served by a biocidal SPC or hybrid; CDP remains defensible where the docking interval is short and first cost dominates. Whatever is selected must be free of the substances controlled under Annex 1 - now including cybutryne - and must be documented so that compliance can be demonstrated.

Limb (a) contains a trap of drafting. It says 'briefly discuss' the Convention and then 'state ALL documents and records'. The word all converts the second half into a checklist, and a checklist is marked by counting items. So the discussion is kept genuinely brief and the documents are written as an explicit list, one line each. A flowing paragraph that mentions the certificate in passing will lose marks that a list would have collected.

Limb (b) names four technologies at two marks each. Each is given mechanism, performance and limitation in that order. Step 8 is not asked for explicitly, but 'discuss various alternatives' invites a comparison, and a short selection paragraph is what distinguishes an engineer's answer from a paint catalogue.

blocks.h: The date of this paper - the trap runs BACKWARDS

blocks.p: This question looks temporally safe, and it is not. The usual temporal danger is importing something that came later. Here the danger is the opposite: leaving out something that had already happened.

Cybutryne controls entered into force on 1 January 2023 - fifteen months before this sitting. Much of the study material on this topic was written when the AFS Convention meant TBT and nothing else, and an answer built from that material describes only the tin position and is incomplete for April 2024. This is worth internalising as a general point: an old paper's correct answer is not always the old answer.

Two further details are specific to this sitting. The 60-month rule was live - ships bearing cybutryne had to remove it or seal it over at the next scheduled renewal after 1 January 2023 and no later than 60 months after the last application. And the transitional period for obtaining a certificate in the amended form was still running, so at this date a ship could legitimately still hold a certificate in the older form.

blocks.h: The one idea that organises limb (b)

blocks.p: There are only two ways to keep a hull clean, and the four named products are variations on them. Either you release a biocide, or you make the surface impossible to grip.

ul: Release a biocide - and then the only question is how well you control the release. CDP dissolves and controls it poorly. SPC hydrolyses and controls it well. Hybrid sits between them. That single axis explains cost, service life, leached-layer thickness and drag for all three.
Make the surface impossible to grip - fouling release. No biocide, lowest drag, but it depends on the ship moving, and the film is soft and expensive.

blocks.p: If you can state that framing in one sentence at the start of limb (b), the four descriptions write themselves and you will not confuse CDP with SPC, which is the commonest error in this topic.

ul: Answering the Convention as a TBT-only instrument. Cybutryne was controlled from 1 January 2023 and was in force at this sitting.
Giving the certificate but forgetting the Record of Anti-Fouling Systems, which is attached to and forms part of it, and the Declaration for the ship between 24 m and 400 GT.
Confusing CDP and SPC. CDP dissolves; SPC hydrolyses and polishes. The biocide is mixed into a CDP binder and chemically bound into an SPC backbone.
Calling fouling release paint an antifouling in the biocidal sense. It contains no biocide; that is its defining feature.
Presenting fouling release as simply the best option. It needs the ship to move, and it is soft, costly and hard to repair.
Writing the organotin dates the wrong way round. 1 January 2003 is when application stopped; 1 January 2008 is when ships had to stop bearing it or seal it over.
Treating 'briefly discuss' as permission to write half the answer on the history of TBT.
'All documents and records'. The examiner is counting. Include the Record, the Declaration, the supporting paint documentation and the survey records - not just the certificate.
Remove OR seal. For both organotins and cybutryne the requirement is a choice: remove the system, or apply a coating forming a barrier over it. Candidates routinely give only removal.
The tonnage and length thresholds. 400 GT and above gets a certificate; 24 m or more but under 400 GT gets a declaration. Expect to be asked what a 30 m, 300 GT ship carries.
Who signs the Declaration. The owner or the owner's authorized agent - not the master, and not a surveyor.
The 60-month rule. It is not a flat deadline: it is the next scheduled renewal after 1 January 2023, subject to an outer limit of 60 months from the last application.
Port State sampling. An officer may do more than read the certificate - a sample of the coating may be taken.
