blocks.p: For limb (a): WHY - WHAT - PROVE IT. Why (TBT harm), what is controlled (organotins 2003 and 2008, cybutryne 2023), and how you prove it (certificate, record, declaration, supporting paperwork, survey records). For the documents, work down by ship size: big ship gets a certificate plus record; small ship gets a declaration plus receipt; everyone keeps the paint paperwork and the survey reports.
For limb (b): DISSOLVE - POLISH - BLEND - SLIP. CDP dissolves, SPC polishes, hybrid blends the two, fouling release is slippery and has no biocide at all.

questions.understand_first: Fouling costs fuel, so ships are painted with something that stops marine growth. For decades that something was tributyl tin, which worked extremely well and turned out to be one of the most damaging substances ever deliberately released into the sea - it deforms shellfish at concentrations measured in parts per trillion. The AFS Convention exists to ban that class of substance and to make a ship prove, on paper, what is actually on her hull. So limb (a) is really two questions: what the Convention prohibits, and what a surveyor or port State officer will ask you to produce. Limb (b) is the engineering consequence - once tin is gone, how else can a coating keep a hull clean? There are only two ideas: keep releasing a biocide in a controlled way, or make the surface so slippery that nothing can hold on. The four named paint types are variations on those two ideas.

blocks.h: 1. a) What a general average act is

blocks.p: The statement in the question is correct, and the features are not a matter of opinion: they are drawn from the definition itself. Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules provides that there is a general average act 'when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure'.

Note first how the Rules apply. They are not law: they take effect by incorporation into the contract of carriage - the bill of lading or charterparty - and the Rule of Interpretation then makes them apply 'to the exclusion of any law and practice inconsistent therewith'. In India the concept is also recognised in the Marine Insurance Act 1963.
Every phrase of Rule A is doing work, and each yields one essential feature:

ol: Extraordinary. The sacrifice or expenditure must be outside the ordinary performance of the contract of carriage. Fuel burned on a normal passage, or wear on machinery in ordinary service, is not extraordinary however costly.

Intentional and voluntary. The loss must be deliberately incurred. Cargo washed overboard by a sea is accidental and lies where it falls; cargo jettisoned by decision is a sacrifice. This is the single feature that most sharply separates general from particular average.
Reasonable. Reinforced by the Rule Paramount, which overrides everything else: 'In no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred.'
Peril. There must be real danger - not necessarily immediate, but genuine and substantial, and more than the ordinary risk of the sea.

Common safety and common adventure. The act must be for the benefit of the whole adventure, not one interest alone, and there must be more than one interest at risk. A ship in ballast with no cargo on board has no common adventure and can have no general average.
Preservation of property. The purpose must be to preserve the property from that peril. Success matters: there must be something saved to contribute.

blocks.h: 3. The lettered rules that qualify the definition

ul: Rule C - only losses which are the direct consequence of the general average act are allowed. It expressly excludes demurrage, loss of market, loss caused by delay and any indirect loss whatsoever, and excludes environmental damage and the consequences of escaping pollutants.

Rule D - rights to contribution are not affected even though the event was due to the fault of one of the parties, without prejudice to any remedies or defences in respect of that fault. So the adjustment proceeds first, and blame is fought separately.
Rule E - the onus of proof is on the party claiming, who must give notice in writing to the average adjuster and supply particulars, generally within twelve months.

blocks.h: 4. How the loss is shared, and what general average is not

blocks.p: Under Rule A.2 the sacrifice is borne by the different contributing interests - ship, cargo and freight at risk - rateably in proportion to their values at the termination of the adventure. The adjustment is prepared by an average adjuster, and security is taken before cargo is released, normally an average bond from the receiver and an average guarantee from the cargo underwriter.

Two distinctions complete the picture. General average is not particular average: particular average is accidental damage, falls on the interest that suffers it and is not shared. And general average is not insurance: it is a rule of contribution between the parties to the adventure, which predates marine insurance entirely, though the contribution is in practice recoverable under the policy.

blocks.h: 5. b) The refloating scenario - the rule that governs it

blocks.p: This situation is dealt with expressly, and by a rule written for exactly these facts. Rule VII, 'Damage to Machinery and Boilers', provides:

'Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.'

blocks.h: 6. Applying it - when the damage is allowed, and when it is not

blocks.p: Yes, the burnt bearings can be allowed in general average - provided four things are shown.

ol: The ship was ashore. She was aground, so the first condition is met on the facts given.

She was in a position of peril. This must be established, not assumed. A vessel lying safely aground on soft mud in fine weather, in no danger and awaiting the tide, is not in peril; one working on a hard bottom, or exposed to weather, tide or the risk of breaking her back, is. This is the condition on which the claim will actually turn.

The machinery was worked with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety. Running the engine ahead and astern to shake her off is precisely that - a deliberate act directed at the safety of the whole adventure, not a routine manoeuvre.

The damage arose at the risk of such damage. The master must have accepted the risk of damaging the engine as the price of refloating. Working an engine hard, astern and ahead, against a grounded hull is known to overload the bearings, and it is that knowing acceptance that makes the loss a sacrifice rather than an accident.

blocks.p: The damage then satisfies Rule A as well: it is extraordinary (not ordinary service), intentional (the engine was deliberately worked in a way likely to damage it), reasonable if refloating was a sensible response, and directed at the common safety. It is also the direct consequence of the act, as Rule C requires. Under Rule D it makes no difference to the right of contribution that the grounding may have been somebody's fault.

The converse must be stated, because it is the trap. Rule VII closes with an absolute prohibition: where the ship is afloat, damage from working the propelling machinery is 'in no circumstances' allowed. So if she had already come off and the bearings burnt while manoeuvring clear, or if she were merely touching and not in peril, the same physical damage would be particular average - the owner's own loss, recoverable if at all under the hull policy and not shared with cargo. The engine damage is identical; the legal answer is opposite; and what decides it is the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked.

Limb (a) is a 'discuss the statement' question, and the highest-scoring way to discuss it is to show that the essential features are not a list somebody invented but the clauses of the Rule A definition read one at a time. That converts a memory answer into an analytical one. Limb (b) is worth the same 8 marks and is decided by a single rule, so the answer must quote Rule VII, apply its four conditions to the facts, and then state the converse. An answer that says 'yes, it is a sacrifice' without naming the rule or testing peril has taken about half the marks available.

blocks.h: Why general average exists at all

blocks.p: It is far older than marine insurance and older than most maritime law - the principle is found in the Rhodian sea law and passed through Roman law into every modern maritime system. The problem it solves is one of incentives at the worst possible moment. If a master must jettison cargo to save the ship, and the loss lay entirely where it fell, then whoever owned that particular cargo would bear everything while the rest of the adventure was saved at his expense. Nobody would consent, and the master's decision would be contested at the moment when hesitation is most dangerous. Making the loss a shared loss removes the conflict: every interest knows that a sacrifice made for the common safety will be contributed to by all. Seen that way, general average is a rule about decision-making under peril, not really a rule about money.

blocks.h: Sacrifice versus accident - the line that decides everything

blocks.p: Almost every general average problem in an examination is a disguised question about whether the loss was chosen. Cargo swept overboard by a sea is an accident; cargo jettisoned is a sacrifice. An engine that fails on passage is an accident; an engine deliberately worked to destruction to refloat the ship is a sacrifice. Water damage from a leak is an accident; water damage from firefighting is a sacrifice. Rule VII is simply that same line drawn for one specific case - and the drafters drew it so firmly that they added an absolute prohibition for the afloat case, because otherwise every hard manoeuvre would generate a claim.

blocks.h: The four conditions of Rule VII, and which one is really in issue

blocks.p: Ashore; in a position of peril; an actual intention to float her for the common safety; at the risk of such damage. In practice the first and third are usually obvious on the facts and the fourth follows from them. The condition that is actually litigated is peril. A ship aground is not automatically in peril - the question is whether she was in real danger, having regard to the bottom, the weather, the tide, her condition and the exposure of the position. That is why a careful answer says the claim 'turns on establishing peril' rather than simply asserting it, and why the master's log, weather records and any surveyor's evidence matter so much afterwards.

blocks.h: Which version of the Rules applies

blocks.p: The York-Antwerp Rules are contractual, not statutory. They apply because the bill of lading or charterparty says they do, which is why the Rule of Interpretation has to declare that they operate 'to the exclusion of any law and practice inconsistent therewith'. The consequence is that the version in force between the parties may be the 1994, 2004 or 2016 text, depending on what the contract incorporates. On this question it does not matter: Rule VII is materially identical in all three. On other questions it can matter a great deal, so the habit of asking which version is incorporated is worth forming.

questions.understand_first: General average is not insurance and not liability - it is a rule of contribution, and it is one of the oldest ideas in maritime law. The problem it solves is a problem of incentives at the worst moment: if the master must sacrifice one interest to save the whole adventure, and the loss lay entirely where it fell, the owner of that interest would be ruined for everyone else's benefit and would fight the decision. Making the loss shared removes the conflict. Everything in limb (a) follows from that purpose - the sacrifice must be deliberate (or there was no decision to protect), for the common safety (or there is nothing to share), and reasonable (or the decision does not deserve protection). And limb (b) is simply that same test applied to an engine: damage suffered because the master chose to risk the machinery to save the ship is a sacrifice; damage suffered in the ordinary course is not.

quick_revision.recall_15s: (a) Rule A: 'There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.' The essential features are the clauses of that sentence: extraordinary - outside the ordinary performance of the contract; intentional and voluntary - deliberately incurred, which is what separates a sacrifice from an accident; reasonable - reinforced by the Rule Paramount, 'In no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred'; peril - real and substantial danger, more than the ordinary risk of the sea; common safety and a common adventure - for the whole adventure and not one interest, so with no cargo on board there is no general average; and preservation of property, so there must be something saved to contribute. Qualifiers: Rule C, only the direct consequence is allowed, and demurrage, loss of market, delay and any indirect loss are excluded; Rule D, the right to contribute is unaffected by the fault of a party, without prejudice to separate remedies; Rule E, the onus of proof is on the claimant, with notice to the average adjuster. Contribution is rateable on the values of ship, cargo and freight at the end of the adventure, adjusted by an average adjuster, with an average bond and average guarantee taken before cargo is released. It is not particular average, which is accidental and lies where it falls, and it is not insurance - it is contribution. The Rules apply by contractual incorporation, not as law. (b) Yes - under Rule VII. 'Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.' Four conditions: she was ashore; she must be shown to have been in peril - the condition that is actually contested; the engine was worked with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety, which working ahead and astern to shake her loose plainly is; and the damage arose at the risk of such damage, the master accepting that risk. The burnt bearings are then an extraordinary, intentional, reasonable sacrifice and the direct consequence of the act. But if she had been afloat, the identical damage would be particular average and the owner's own loss.

quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (b) 'yes, it is a general average sacrifice' without naming Rule VII, without testing whether the ship was in a position of peril, and without stating the converse. Rule VII allows the claim only where the ship is ashore and in peril and the machinery was worked with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety at the risk of such damage - and it then prohibits absolutely, 'in any circumstances', any allowance for machinery damage caused by working the propelling machinery while the ship is afloat. The same burnt bearings are therefore general average or particular average according to the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked. A second trap in limb (a) is forgetting that there must be a common adventure: a ship in ballast with no cargo has no general average, because there is no other interest to contribute.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the general average question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What a general average act is - the Rule A definition. 2 The essential features drawn from it. 3 The qualifying lettered rules C, D and E. 4 How the loss is shared, and what general average is not. 5 The refloating scenario and Rule VII. 6 Applying Rule VII to the facts, with the converse.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the Rule A definition of a general average act.
retrieval_cards.answer: There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
retrieval_cards.why: The essential features are the clauses of this sentence. Quote it and the features write themselves.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the essential difference between general average and particular average?
retrieval_cards.answer: General average loss is intentionally and reasonably incurred for the common safety of the whole adventure, and is shared rateably by all the contributing interests. Particular average is accidental damage which falls on the interest that suffers it and is not shared. The dividing line is whether the loss was chosen.
retrieval_cards.why: Almost every general average problem is a disguised question about whether the loss was deliberate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Quote Rule VII of the York-Antwerp Rules.
retrieval_cards.answer: Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.
retrieval_cards.why: It decides limb (b) outright. The second half - the absolute prohibition when afloat - is the part candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A grounded vessel's main engine bearings burn out while working ahead and astern to refloat her. Is the damage general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, under Rule VII, provided four things are shown: that she was ashore; that she was in a position of peril; that the machinery was worked with an actual intention to float her for the common safety; and that the damage arose at the risk of such damage. Working ahead and astern to shake her loose establishes the intention and the acceptance of risk. Peril is the condition that must actually be proved.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner asks for justification, so the marks are in applying the four conditions rather than in the yes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Would the answer change if the ship had already been afloat when the bearings burnt?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, completely. Rule VII provides that where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average. The identical damage would be particular average - the owner's own loss, recoverable if at all under the hull policy and not shared with cargo.
retrieval_cards.why: Same physical damage, opposite legal answer. What decides it is the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The grounding was caused by the master's negligence. Does that defeat the general average claim?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Rule D provides that rights to contribution in general average shall not be affected though the event which gave rise to the sacrifice may have been due to the fault of one of the parties to the common maritime adventure, but without prejudice to any remedies or defences open against or to that party in respect of that fault. The adjustment proceeds; blame is dealt with separately.
retrieval_cards.why: It keeps the adjustment moving. Cargo interests can still sue the owner for the fault - they simply cannot use it to refuse to contribute.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship is in ballast with no cargo on board and you sacrifice equipment to save her. Is there general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Rule A requires the act to be for the common safety and for the purpose of preserving property involved in a common maritime adventure. With no cargo there is only one interest at risk, no common adventure and nothing to contribute, so the loss falls entirely on the owner.
retrieval_cards.why: The word common in the definition is a condition, not decoration, and this is the quickest way to test whether it has been understood.

blocks.h: 1. A) What the human element means in STCW

blocks.p: STCW refuses to treat competence as something that time served automatically confers. It replaces experience with demonstrated competence, and then addresses the conditions - fitness, rest, teamwork and company responsibility - under which competence can actually be exercised. The instrument is the STCW Convention and Code, 1978, as amended, most significantly by the Manila amendments of 2010, in force from 1 January 2012.

ul: The Part A tables of competence specify, for every function and level, the competence required, the knowledge, understanding and proficiency behind it, the methods for demonstrating it and the criteria for evaluating it - so assessment is against a published standard, not an examiner's impression.
Part A is mandatory; Part B is guidance - a distinction worth stating explicitly.

The Manila amendments added mandatory training in leadership and teamworking at operational level and leadership and managerial skill at management level - where engine-room and bridge resource management, situational awareness and workload management enter the Convention. It is the explicit recognition that technically competent individuals still fail as a team.
Regulation I/6 governs training and assessment, and regulation I/8 requires a quality standards system, so the training system itself is audited rather than assumed.
Regulation I/11 requires periodic revalidation, and chapter VI mandatory safety familiarisation and basic training before a seafarer is assigned duties.

blocks.h: 3. Fitness for duty - the physical human being

ul: Regulation VIII/1 requires each Administration, for the purpose of preventing fatigue, to establish and enforce rest periods for watchkeeping personnel and for those with designated safety, security and pollution-prevention duties in accordance with section A-VIII/1, and to require that watch systems are arranged so that efficiency is not impaired by fatigue.

The Manila-amended A-VIII/1 minimum rest is 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. The daily rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.

Authorised exceptions are tightly conditioned: weekly rest may not fall below 70 hours in any 7-day period, exceptions from the 77-hour norm may not run for more than two consecutive weeks, and daily rest may then be divided into no more than three periods.
The Manila amendments also introduced alcohol limits for masters, officers and other seafarers with designated safety, security and environmental duties.
Regulation I/9 sets medical fitness standards, and regulation VIII/2 with section A-VIII/2 governs watchkeeping arrangements and principles.

blocks.h: 4. Responsibility placed on companies and Administrations

blocks.p: Regulation I/14 makes the company responsible for ensuring that seafarers hold valid certificates, are familiarised with their duties and with the ship's arrangements, and that documentation is maintained - so the human element is not left as an individual's problem. Administrations operate quality standards systems and are subject to independent evaluation and reporting to IMO.

blocks.h: 5. B) The IMO guidance on fatigue

blocks.p: The guidance is MSC.1/Circ.1598, 'Guidelines on fatigue', of 24 January 2019, approved at the 100th session of the Maritime Safety Committee and finalized by the HTW Sub-Committee. It supersedes MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory, not mandatory - the binding rest-hour requirements remain in STCW chapter VIII and in MLC 2006. The Guidelines are arranged in six modules, each addressed to a different party:

ul: Module 1 - Fatigue: what it is and its causes, grouped as sleep and rest, the biological clock and circadian rhythm, health and stress, environmental factors such as noise, vibration and motion, sleep disorders and operational factors. It defines sleep debt as insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods.
Module 2 - Fatigue and the Company: assessing, mitigating and managing fatigue risk in the safety management system, in manning decisions and in scheduling.

Module 3 - Fatigue and the Seafarer: practical guidance for the master, officers and ratings on sleep quality, diet and the limits of countermeasures - notably that caffeine is not a substitute for sleep.
Module 4 - Fatigue Awareness and Training.
Module 5 - Fatigue and Ship Design: mitigation designed in - accommodation location, noise, vibration, lighting and habitability.
Module 6 - Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities: how regulators and inspectors should approach it.

blocks.h: 6. How the guidance and the rules fit together

blocks.p: The Guidelines are explicit that hours of rest are set by a prescriptive formula in STCW chapter VIII, and that complying with the formula is not the same as being rested: managers must allow for circadian rhythm and sleep debt, and - in the Guidelines' own words - rest means rest, not the substitution of a different form of work. The same theme runs through MLC 2006 Regulations 2.3, 2.4 and 2.7. A management-level engineer should therefore treat recorded compliance as the floor, and a rest-hour record that is always exactly compliant as a warning rather than a reassurance.

Two printed limbs of 8 marks each, so split the answer evenly and head each limb clearly. Limb A rewards structure - competence tables, fitness for duty, company responsibility - and limb B rewards naming the actual circular. A candidate who writes generally about tiredness for the second limb without producing MSC.1/Circ.1598 and its module structure will lose most of eight marks, because 'the IMO guidance' is a specific document.

blocks.h: The organising idea for limb A

blocks.p: STCW attacks the human element on three fronts, and saying so gives the limb a spine: can they do it (competence standards, assessed against published criteria), are they fit to do it now (fitness for duty - rest, medical, alcohol), and who is responsible for making that possible (regulation I/14, the company). The Manila amendments strengthened all three and added the fourth dimension the older Convention lacked - can they work as a team, through mandatory leadership and teamworking training.

blocks.h: The numbers you must get right

blocks.p: 10 hours in any 24, and 77 hours in any 7 days. Divided into no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rest periods. Exceptions may not go below 70 hours in any 7 days and may not run more than two consecutive weeks. Learn 10, 77, 2, 6, 14, 70 - and be careful, because 70 and 77 are both real figures doing different jobs: 77 is the norm, 70 is the floor under an authorised exception. Quoting 70 as the normal requirement is the classic error, and it is exactly the trap that a pre-2010 copy of the Code will lead you into.

This is worth a paragraph of its own because it caught this project. A freely available IMO circular copy of section A-VIII/1 - STCW.6/Circ.1 - reproduces the 1995 Code: five paragraphs, 70 hours weekly, and no 14-hour interval provision at all. It looks entirely authoritative, it is on an official domain, and it is superseded. A candidate who revises from it will write 70 where 77 is required and will omit the 14-hour rule altogether. The lesson generalises: for any instrument that has been amended, the question to ask of a source is not 'is this official?' but 'which edition is this?'

questions.understand_first: The phrase human element is not a polite word for human error. In STCW it means the whole set of conditions that decide whether a competent person actually performs competently on the day - whether the standard he was assessed against was published and objective, whether he has slept, whether he is medically fit, whether he can work as part of a team, and whether his company has made any of that possible. That is why limb A cannot be answered with rest hours alone: rest is one of four fronts. And it is why limb B is a separate document - the mandatory rule sets a floor for hours, while the Guidelines address the thing the floor cannot reach, which is whether the person is actually rested.

quick_revision.recall_15s: (A) Human element in STCW. The instrument is STCW 1978 as amended, above all by the Manila amendments of 2010, in force 1 January 2012. It replaces time served with demonstrated competence, then secures the conditions in which competence can be exercised. Competence: the Part A tables give, for each function and level, the competence, the knowledge, understanding and proficiency, the methods of demonstrating and the criteria for evaluating - and Part A is mandatory while Part B is guidance. Manila added mandatory leadership and teamworking at operational level and leadership and managerial skill at management level, bringing engine-room and bridge resource management into the Convention. reg I/6 training and assessment, I/8 quality standards, I/11 revalidation, chapter VI familiarisation before duties. Fitness for duty: reg VIII/1 requires Administrations, to prevent fatigue, to establish and enforce rest periods per section A-VIII/1 - 10 hours in any 24 and 77 hours in any 7 days, in no more than two periods one of at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rests. Authorised exceptions may not fall below 70 hours weekly, may not run beyond two consecutive weeks, and allow no more than three daily periods. Manila also added alcohol limits; reg I/9 sets medical standards and reg VIII/2 watchkeeping arrangements. Responsibility: reg I/14 puts valid certification, familiarisation and documentation on the company; Administrations run quality standards subject to independent evaluation. (B) Fatigue guidance. MSC.1/Circ.1598, 'Guidelines on fatigue', 24 January 2019, approved at MSC 100, superseding MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory; the binding rest hours stay in STCW chapter VIII and MLC 2006. Six modules: 1 Fatigue and its causes, defining sleep debt; 2 the Company; 3 the Seafarer; 4 Awareness and Training; 5 Ship Design; 6 the Administration and Port State Authorities. How they fit: hours of rest are a prescriptive formula, and compliance is not the same as being rested - allow for circadian rhythm and sleep debt, and treat an always-exactly-compliant record as a warning.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the human element and fatigue question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the human element means in STCW. 2 Competence-based standards. 3 Fitness for duty. 4 Responsibility on companies and Administrations. 5 The IMO guidance on fatigue - MSC.1/Circ.1598 and its six modules. 6 How the guidance and the mandatory rules fit together.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 1 to 4 are limb A's 8 marks, steps 5 and 6 limb B's. Keeping competence in A and the Guidelines in B stops the two limbs duplicating each other.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the minimum hours of rest under the Manila-amended section A-VIII/1.
retrieval_cards.answer: Not less than 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. The daily rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.
retrieval_cards.why: The 14-hour interval is the provision most often omitted, and its absence from a source is the quickest way to tell that the source is pre-Manila.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the weekly minimum rest 70 hours or 77 hours?
retrieval_cards.answer: 77 hours in any 7-day period is the norm. 70 hours is the floor that applies only where an exception has been authorised, and such an exception may not run for more than two consecutive weeks. Both figures are real; they do different jobs.
retrieval_cards.why: A widely available official IMO circular copy of A-VIII/1 is the pre-Manila 1995 text and gives 70 as the weekly figure. It is official and superseded - always check the edition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which circular is the IMO guidance on fatigue, and what did it replace?
retrieval_cards.answer: MSC.1/Circ.1598, Guidelines on fatigue, dated 24 January 2019 and approved at the 100th session of the Maritime Safety Committee. It supersedes MSC/Circ.1014 on Guidance on fatigue mitigation and management, approved at MSC 74 in 2001. It is recommendatory, not mandatory.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb B says 'the IMO guidance' - a specific document. Naming it and its predecessor is most of the eight marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the six modules of MSC.1/Circ.1598.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Fatigue - what it is and its causes. 2 Fatigue and the Company. 3 Fatigue and the Seafarer. 4 Fatigue Awareness and Training. 5 Fatigue and Ship Design. 6 Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities.
retrieval_cards.why: Each module is addressed to a different party, which is the structural point: fatigue is managed by the company, the individual, the designer and the regulator, not only by the watchkeeper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What did the Manila amendments add to STCW on the human element?
retrieval_cards.answer: Mandatory training in leadership and teamworking at operational level and in leadership and managerial skill at management level - bringing engine-room and bridge resource management, situational awareness and workload management into the Convention; revised and tightened rest-hour requirements in section A-VIII/1 including the 14-hour interval rule; and alcohol limits for masters, officers and seafarers with designated safety, security and environmental duties.
retrieval_cards.why: The teamworking addition is the recognition that technically competent individuals still fail as a crew, which is the analytical heart of limb A.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your engineer's rest-hour record is exactly compliant every single week. Is that reassuring?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - it is a warning. The Guidelines are explicit that hours of rest are a prescriptive formula and that complying with the formula is not the same as being rested; circadian rhythm and sleep debt determine whether rest is restorative. A record that is always exactly at the limit suggests the limit is driving the record rather than the work.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the management-level judgement the question is really testing, and it is what separates a Class I answer from a recitation of numbers.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does STCW regulation I/14 require of the company?
retrieval_cards.answer: That seafarers assigned to its ships hold valid certificates, are familiarised with their specific duties and with the ship's arrangements, installations, equipment and procedures before being assigned duties, and that documentation and data are maintained. It places the human element on the company rather than leaving it as an individual's problem.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb A is incomplete without the responsibility front, and I/14 is the provision that supplies it.

blocks.p: A survey is an examination of the ship herself - her structure, machinery, equipment and arrangements - against prescriptive technical requirements, to establish that her physical condition satisfies the relevant convention. A safety management audit is a systematic, independent and documented examination of the management system, using objective evidence to establish whether the procedures required by the ISM Code exist, are understood, are implemented and are effective.

Put shortly: a survey looks at the ship; an audit looks at the system and the people who run it. A survey verifies condition and reports deficiencies; an audit verifies management and reports non-conformities and observations.

blocks.h: 2. b) The position of the recognized organization

blocks.p: The four scenarios below all turn on one point. Under the 2023 Guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations the Administration is responsible for verifying compliance with the Code and for issuing the Document of Compliance to companies and the Safety Management Certificate to ships. A recognized organization acts only under a written authorization from that Administration, and where an Administration authorizes an organization to issue these certificates on its behalf, the RO Code (mandatory through SOLAS regulation XI-1/1) and the III Code apply.

So the RO makes the technical judgements that verification requires - is this a non-conformity, is it major, has corrective action been taken. It does not have authority to alter the terms on which the flag State certified the ship. That distinction decides limbs (iii) and (iv).

blocks.h: 3. Where there is evidence of a major non-conformity

blocks.p: A major non-conformity is an identifiable deviation posing a serious threat to the safety of personnel or the ship, or a serious risk to the environment, requiring immediate corrective action, and it includes the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the Code.

ul: A certificate must not be issued, and an existing certificate must not be endorsed for annual or intermediate verification.
The finding must be downgraded to a non-conformity by immediate corrective action before the certificate can be acted on; otherwise the certificate is withdrawn.
The RO reports to the Administration and acts under the documented procedures its certification scheme is required to hold for actions in cases of major non-conformity.

After a withdrawal, an interim certificate must not be issued in its place, and a new DOC or SMC is issued only after an initial verification, or an additional verification of the extent and scope of an initial verification.
Failure to take adequate corrective action, including measures to prevent recurrence, may itself be considered a major non-conformity.

blocks.p: An ordinary non-conformity is an observed situation where objective evidence shows a specified requirement has not been fulfilled, but without the serious threat that makes it major. The consequences are materially different.

ul: The certificate may still be issued or endorsed.
The company - not the RO - is responsible for determining and initiating the corrective action needed to correct the non-conformity or its cause.
Corrective actions and any subsequent audits are completed within the time period agreed; for corrective actions this should not normally exceed three months.
The company applies for the follow-up audits as agreed.
The findings are recorded in the audit report, a copy of which goes to the company.
Failure to correct non-conformities with specific requirements of the Code may affect the validity of the Document of Compliance and the related Safety Management Certificates.

blocks.h: 5. Where an extension of the Safety Management Certificate is requested

blocks.p: Neither the ISM Code nor the 2023 Guidelines contains a general power to extend a Safety Management Certificate. The Code provides for renewal verification before expiry, and fixes the validity of the new certificate where renewal is completed within three months before expiry - but that is a renewal, not an extension.

It follows that the RO has nothing of its own to grant. The request lies outside the delegated verification function, and the RO's action is to refer it to the Administration, which alone may decide what to do with a certificate it issued, and to act only on the Administration's specific instruction. The RO advises the company that the proper course is to apply for renewal verification before the certificate expires, and records the request and the referral.

blocks.h: 6. Where revision of an entry on a certificate is requested

blocks.p: The entries on a DOC or SMC record what the flag State certified - the company and its address, the ship, the ship types covered. The RO issues on the Administration's behalf and so may not amend that record on its own authority. Its first action is to establish which kind of change is being asked for.

ul: Administrative - a change of company name or address, or of ship name, where the underlying facts of certification are unchanged. The RO verifies the change is genuine and supported, refers it to the Administration, and on its authority the certificate is reissued with the corrected entry and the original expiry date retained.

Substantive - a change of the company actually responsible for operating the ship, a change of flag, or the addition of a ship type not covered by the DOC. These are not revisions at all. They require fresh verification and a new certificate, with an interim certificate issued to cover the intervening period where the criteria for one are met.

blocks.p: In both cases the RO records the change and reports it to the Administration; it does not simply amend the certificate in hand.

blocks.h: 7. c) When the DOC and the SMC may be invalidated

blocks.p: The Document of Compliance may be withdrawn or cease to be valid where:

ul: the annual verification is not requested - it must be carried out within three months before or after each anniversary date;
there is evidence of major non-conformity with the Code;
it expires without renewal verification having been completed;
the company changes - the DOC is issued to a company, not to a ship;
the company is found to be operating ship types not stated on it, or has stopped operating a type, so that appropriate action is required.

blocks.p: The Safety Management Certificate may be withdrawn or cease to be valid where:

ul: the Document of Compliance is withdrawn - all associated Safety Management Certificates and interim certificates are withdrawn with it, and this is the trigger candidates most often miss;
the intermediate verification is not requested - at least one is required between the second and third anniversary dates;
there is evidence of major non-conformity with the Code;
it expires without renewal verification;
the ship changes flag, or the company responsible for her operation changes, so that the certificate no longer records the true position.

blocks.p: Underlying all of these, failure to correct non-conformities may affect the validity of the Document of Compliance and the related Safety Management Certificates, and failure to take adequate corrective action may itself be treated as a major non-conformity - which then engages the withdrawal triggers above.

The marks are 2 + 8 + 6 and the answer is shaped to them. Limb (a) is two marks: one clean distinction, no padding. Limb (b) is four scenarios at two marks each, so each gets a short, specific list of actions rather than an essay. Limb (c) is six marks and is written as two separate lists, DOC and SMC, because the triggers differ and a single merged list loses the one point the examiner is most likely to be looking for.

Step 2 is not in the printed question and is the reason the answer holds together. Establishing that the RO acts only under delegated authority before you answer the four scenarios turns limbs (iii) and (iv) from guesswork into a deduction.

blocks.h: The edition point - and why it matters at this sitting

blocks.p: The IMO guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations were replaced by resolution A.1188(33), the 2023 Guidelines, adopted on 6 December 2023. Its operative paragraph 5 revokes resolution A.1118(30) - the 2017 revision, which had stood for six years and which almost all circulating study material cites.

At the date of this paper the 2023 Guidelines had been the current edition for four months. Citing A.1118(30) here is a wrong-edition error. It is a dangerous one because the substance of the paragraphs used in this answer is largely unchanged between the two, so the answer still reads correctly - only the authority is wrong. The 33rd Assembly of December 2023 is a standing edition boundary for every 2024 sitting: check any Assembly-adopted guideline you are about to cite in a 2024 paper against it.

blocks.h: The idea that makes limb (b) easy

blocks.p: Ask who owns the decision. The Administration is responsible for verifying compliance and issuing the certificates; the RO only acts under a written authorization. So split the four scenarios in two:

ul: (i) and (ii) are technical findings. Deciding whether something is a non-conformity, whether it is major, and whether corrective action is adequate is exactly what the RO was authorized to do. The RO acts.

(iii) and (iv) are changes to the terms of certification. Extending a certificate or altering an entry on it changes what the flag State certified. The RO has no authority of its own and refers to the Administration.

blocks.p: If you can state that split, you can construct both halves of limb (b) even under pressure, and you will avoid the common error of inventing a rule that lets the RO extend a certificate on its own.

ul: Citing A.1118(30). It was revoked on 6 December 2023, four months before this paper.
Treating a major non-conformity as merely a worse ordinary one. The consequence is categorical: the certificate cannot be issued or endorsed, where an ordinary non-conformity does not stop it.
Saying the RO corrects the non-conformity. The company determines and initiates corrective action; the RO verifies it.
Forgetting that withdrawing the DOC withdraws all the associated SMCs. This is the single highest-value point in limb (c).

Inventing an extension provision for the SMC. There is none in the Code or the Guidelines. Saying so, and referring the request to the Administration, is the correct answer and a stronger one than a fabricated rule.
Confusing revision of an entry with a change of company or flag. The first is a correction to the record; the second needs fresh verification and a new certificate.
Writing limb (a) at length. It is worth two marks.

The three-month figure appears twice and means different things. Corrective action should normally not exceed three months; annual verification of the DOC is carried out within three months before or after the anniversary date. Do not merge them.

Anniversary versus expiry. Annual verification runs off the anniversary date; the intermediate verification of the SMC falls between the second and third anniversary dates. Work backwards from the expiry date when you check one.
'Invalidated' is broader than 'withdrawn'. A certificate can cease to be effective by expiry, or by the facts on it ceasing to be true, without anyone withdrawing it. Answer both.

Who issues, who verifies. An examiner may press on whether the RO or the Administration withdraws a certificate. The Administration withdraws it, or the Contracting Government which issued it does so at the Administration's request.
Interim certificates after a withdrawal. Expect the follow-up: no, an interim certificate is not the way back after a withdrawal for a major non-conformity.
Define a major non-conformity. How does it differ from a non-conformity?
You find a major non-conformity during an SMC audit. What happens to the ship?
Can the major non-conformity be downgraded, and by what?
Who withdraws a Document of Compliance, and on what grounds?
If the DOC is withdrawn, what happens to the ships' certificates?
When is the intermediate verification of the SMC carried out?
A company asks you to extend the SMC by a month. What do you do?
The company has changed its registered address. Is a new certificate needed?
Which resolution carries the current guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations?

blocks.p: For limb (b), remember DECIDE or REFER. Findings - major and ordinary - the RO decides. Certificate terms - extension and entries - the RO refers. For limb (c), remember that the DOC is the parent: kill the DOC and every SMC dies with it. Then each certificate has the same two triggers of its own - verification not requested, and evidence of a major non-conformity - plus expiry and a change in the facts recorded on it.

questions.understand_first: This question is about WHO may do WHAT to a certificate. A recognized organization does not have authority of its own: it acts under a written authorization from the flag State, and the Administration remains responsible for verifying compliance and for issuing the Document of Compliance and the Safety Management Certificate. Everything in limb (b) follows from that one idea. Where the ISM Code or the Administration's guidelines give the RO a technical decision to make - is this a non-conformity, is it major, has corrective action been taken - the RO decides. Where the request is to change the terms on which the flag State certified something - extend it, alter an entry on it - the RO has nothing to decide and refers it to the Administration. Limb (c) is then just the list of ways a certificate stops being good, and almost all of them come out of section 13 of the Code itself.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three separate demands. (a) a two-mark definitional distinction between audit and survey. (b) four short procedural answers, each on what the RO actually DOES. (c) an enumeration of the circumstances in which the DOC and the SMC may be invalidated. The question is testing certification machinery, not the content of a safety management system.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish an audit from a survey.
retrieval_cards.answer: A survey examines the ship - structure, machinery and equipment - against prescriptive technical requirements and reports deficiencies. An audit is a systematic, independent and documented examination of the management system, using objective evidence to establish whether procedures exist, are implemented and are effective, and reports non-conformities and observations.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a major non-conformity?
retrieval_cards.answer: An identifiable deviation posing a serious threat to the safety of personnel or the ship, or a serious risk to the environment, requiring immediate corrective action, and including the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the ISM Code.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the RO do where there is evidence of a major non-conformity?
retrieval_cards.answer: The certificate must not be issued and an existing certificate must not be endorsed. The finding must be downgraded by immediate corrective action or the certificate is withdrawn. The RO reports to the Administration and follows its documented procedures. After a withdrawal no interim certificate is issued, and a new certificate requires an initial verification or an additional verification of the extent and scope of an initial verification.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens where ordinary non-conformities are found?
retrieval_cards.answer: The certificate may still be issued or endorsed. The company determines and initiates the corrective action needed to correct the non-conformity or its cause. Corrective actions and follow-up audits are completed within an agreed period, for corrective action normally not exceeding three months, and the company applies for the follow-up audit. Failure to correct may affect the validity of the DOC and related SMCs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A company asks the RO to extend the Safety Management Certificate. What is the answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: Neither the ISM Code nor the 2023 Guidelines provides a power to extend an SMC, so the RO has nothing of its own to grant. It refers the request to the Administration and acts only on its specific instruction, advising the company that the proper course is renewal verification completed before expiry. Do not invent an extension provision.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the RO do when revision of an entry on a certificate is requested?
retrieval_cards.answer: Establish whether the change is administrative or substantive. Administrative - company name or address, ship name - is verified and referred to the Administration, and the certificate is reissued with the corrected entry and the original expiry date retained. Substantive - change of company, change of flag, or a new ship type - is not a revision: it needs fresh verification and a new certificate, with an interim certificate where the criteria are met.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On what grounds may the Document of Compliance be withdrawn, and what follows?
retrieval_cards.answer: Where the annual verification is not requested, or where there is evidence of major non-conformity with the Code - ISM Code 13.5. All associated Safety Management Certificates and Interim Safety Management Certificates are withdrawn with it - 13.5.1.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On what grounds may the Safety Management Certificate be withdrawn?
retrieval_cards.answer: Where the intermediate verification is not requested, or where there is evidence of major non-conformity with the Code - ISM Code 13.9 - and in addition whenever the Document of Compliance is withdrawn. It also ceases to be effective on expiry without renewal, or where the ship changes flag or the operating company changes.

retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1188(33), the 2023 Guidelines, adopted on 6 December 2023. Its paragraph 5 revokes resolution A.1118(30), the 2017 revision, which had stood for six years.

blocks.p: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, 1982, entered into force on 16 November 1994 and is properly described as the constitution of the oceans. Part XII is devoted to the protection and preservation of the marine environment, and its highlights are these:

ul: A general obligation on all States to protect and preserve the marine environment. It is a free-standing duty, owed generally and not only to neighbours.

The sovereign right to exploit natural resources is expressly qualified by it. States may exploit their resources pursuant to their own environmental policies, but in accordance with the duty to protect and preserve.

A duty to take all measures necessary to prevent, reduce and control pollution of the marine environment from any source, using the best practicable means at their disposal and in accordance with their capabilities.

A duty not to transfer damage or hazards from one area to another, and not to transform one type of pollution into another. This is a sophisticated provision and a good one to quote - it prevents a State from solving its own problem by exporting it.
A duty to prevent the intentional or accidental introduction of alien or new species which may cause significant and harmful changes - the provision that underlies the whole ballast water regime.

blocks.h: 2. a) Every source of pollution is covered

blocks.p: A frequently missed highlight is the breadth of Part XII. It is not a shipping instrument. It requires States to adopt laws and take measures addressing pollution:

ul: from land-based sources, including rivers, estuaries, pipelines and outfalls;
from seabed activities subject to national jurisdiction, and from activities in the Area - the deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction;
by dumping, which requires the express prior approval of the coastal State;
from vessels;
from or through the atmosphere.

blocks.p: Land-based sources contribute the greater part of marine pollution, and an answer which treats UNCLOS as being about ships alone has missed the point of the Part.

blocks.h: 3. a) Standards, and the role of the IMO

blocks.p: For pollution from vessels UNCLOS does something structurally important: it does not set technical standards itself. States are to act through the competent international organization - in practice the IMO - to establish international rules and standards, and national laws must have at least the same effect as those international rules.

This is the hinge of the whole system. It is why UNCLOS contains no discharge limits and no construction standards, and why MARPOL exists. UNCLOS allocates the authority; the IMO instruments supply the content.
UNCLOS then distributes enforcement three ways, which is one of its most practical features:

ul: Flag State - must ensure compliance by ships flying its flag wherever the violation occurs, and must provide for effective enforcement irrespective of where it happened.

Port State - may investigate and, where the evidence warrants, institute proceedings in respect of a discharge, including one occurring outside its own waters. This is the basis of the port State control system.

Coastal State - may act in respect of violations within its territorial sea or exclusive economic zone, with the powers graduated according to the seriousness of the harm, ranging from requiring information to inspection and detention.

blocks.p: Beyond enforcement, Part XII provides for global and regional cooperation, immediate notification to States likely to be affected by imminent or actual damage, contingency plans, monitoring and environmental impact assessment, and scientific and technical assistance to developing States. It preserves the right of a State to intervene beyond the territorial sea to protect its coastline after a maritime casualty; it establishes responsibility and liability for damage caused by breach of these obligations; it gives coastal States special powers in ice-covered areas; and it preserves sovereign immunity for warships and other State ships on non-commercial service, while requiring States to ensure such ships act so far as reasonable in a manner consistent with the Convention.

All the zones are measured from the baseline - normally the low-water line along the coast, with straight baselines permitted where the coast is deeply indented or fringed with islands. Waters landward of the baseline are internal waters.

The territorial sea extends up to 12 nautical miles from the baseline. The coastal State has full sovereignty over it, extending to the airspace above and to the seabed and subsoil below. That sovereignty is subject to one major qualification: the right of innocent passage enjoyed by ships of all States. Passage must be continuous and expeditious and must not be prejudicial to the peace, good order or security of the coastal State.
A zone contiguous to the territorial sea, extending up to 24 nautical miles from the baseline - that is, a further 12 miles beyond the territorial sea.

It is not an area of sovereignty. The coastal State may exercise only the control necessary to prevent infringement of its customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary laws and regulations within its territory or territorial sea, and to punish such infringement where it has already been committed there. The four subjects are the whole of it - it confers no general policing power.

An area beyond and adjacent to the territorial sea extending up to 200 nautical miles from the baseline. The distinction that carries the marks is between sovereignty and sovereign rights: in the EEZ the coastal State has sovereign rights, not sovereignty, and they are resource rights.

ul: Sovereign rights for exploring, exploiting, conserving and managing the natural resources, living and non-living, of the waters superjacent to the seabed and of the seabed and its subsoil, and for other economic exploitation such as the production of energy from water, currents and winds.
Jurisdiction over artificial islands, installations and structures; marine scientific research; and the protection and preservation of the marine environment.
Other States retain the freedoms of navigation and overflight and of the laying of submarine cables and pipelines. A merchant ship transits an EEZ as of right.

blocks.p: The continental shelf is the seabed and subsoil of the submarine areas beyond the territorial sea - not the water column above it, which is the distinction from the EEZ. Its extent is defined two ways, and the coastal State takes the greater:

ul: throughout the natural prolongation of its land territory to the outer edge of the continental margin; or
to a distance of 200 nautical miles from the baseline where the outer edge of the margin does not extend that far.

blocks.p: Where the margin extends beyond 200 miles the outer limit is constrained - it may not exceed 350 nautical miles from the baselines, or 100 nautical miles from the 2,500 metre isobath. The coastal State has sovereign rights for the purpose of exploring it and exploiting its natural resources. Two points distinguish a good answer: these rights are exclusive and exist automatically, without any need for occupation or express proclamation; and they do not affect the legal status of the waters above or of the airspace.

All parts of the sea not included in the exclusive economic zone, the territorial sea, the internal waters of a State, or archipelagic waters. They are open to all States, coastal and land-locked alike, and no State may validly purport to subject any part of them to its sovereignty. They are reserved for peaceful purposes.

The freedoms of the high seas include navigation, overflight, the laying of submarine cables and pipelines, the construction of artificial islands, fishing, and scientific research, each exercised with due regard for the interests of other States.

Jurisdiction rests with the flag State, which must exercise effective administrative, technical and social control over its ships. The recognised exceptions are important: piracy, which any State may act against; the right of visit where there is reasonable ground to suspect piracy, slave trading, unauthorised broadcasting or statelessness; and hot pursuit from a coastal State's waters, which must be continuous and ends the moment the pursued ship enters the territorial sea of its own or a third State. There is also a general duty to render assistance to any person in danger of being lost at sea.

Limb (b) names five zones for eight marks, so each is worth about a mark and a half and each gets three things and no more: the limit, the legal character, and the principal right. Writing a page on the territorial sea and one line on the continental shelf is how this limb is normally lost.

Limb (a) says 'important highlights', which is an invitation to structure. Four structured highlights - the general duty, the breadth of sources, the deferral to the IMO, and the three-way enforcement - score better than one continuous paragraph on the duty to protect, however well written. The word highlights is asking you to select and organise, and that selection is itself being marked.

blocks.h: The one idea that carries limb (b)

blocks.p: Coastal State power decreases with distance, in stages. Do not learn five definitions; learn one gradient:

ul: Internal waters - full sovereignty, no right of passage at all.
Territorial sea, 12 miles - full sovereignty, but qualified by innocent passage.
Contiguous zone, 24 miles - no sovereignty; only control, and only over four named subjects.
EEZ, 200 miles - sovereign rights over resources, plus jurisdiction over three named matters; navigation stays free.
Continental shelf - sovereign rights over the seabed only; the water above is unaffected.
High seas - no sovereignty at all; flag State jurisdiction only.

blocks.p: Said that way the answer is one idea rather than five, and the distances 12, 24 and 200 sit on it naturally. Note also that every one of them is measured from the baseline, not from the shoreline - the contiguous zone is 24 miles from the baseline, not 24 beyond the territorial sea.
UNCLOS itself is stable: in force since 16 November 1994, and neither the zone provisions nor Part XII has changed. There is, however, one live boundary.

The BBNJ Agreement - the agreement under UNCLOS on the conservation and sustainable use of marine biological diversity of areas beyond national jurisdiction, sometimes called the High Seas Treaty - was adopted on 19 June 2023, which is before this sitting, and opened for signature in September 2023. It did not enter into force until well after this paper. So at this sitting it may properly be mentioned as adopted and awaiting entry into force, and it is a good closing sentence for limb (a) if you have time - but it must never be written as applying. Adopted, in force and applying are three different states, and collapsing them is one of the commonest and most costly errors in a law answer.

ul: Measuring the contiguous zone from the outer edge of the territorial sea. It is 24 miles from the baseline, which is 12 beyond the territorial sea.
Saying the coastal State has sovereignty in the EEZ. It has sovereign rights over resources - a materially different thing, and the examiner is watching for the word.
Confusing the continental shelf with the EEZ. The shelf is the seabed and subsoil; it says nothing about the water above.
Treating Part XII as being about ships. It covers land-based sources, seabed activities, the Area, dumping, vessels and the atmosphere.
Expecting to find discharge standards in UNCLOS. It sets none - it directs States to act through the competent international organization, which is why MARPOL exists.
Giving only flag State enforcement. Port State and coastal State enforcement are both express, and the port State power over discharges outside its own waters is the striking one.
Writing the BBNJ Agreement as being in force at this sitting. It was adopted before the paper and in force long after it.
Sovereignty versus sovereign rights. The single highest-value distinction in the whole question. Territorial sea - sovereignty. EEZ and shelf - sovereign rights.
The four contiguous-zone subjects. Customs, fiscal, immigration, sanitary. Expect to be asked to name them, and expect no credit for a general 'law enforcement' answer.
'Do the shelf rights need to be claimed?' No - they exist automatically and exclusively, without occupation or proclamation. A favourite follow-up.
Innocent passage. What makes passage not innocent, and does it apply in the EEZ? In the EEZ the freedom of navigation applies, which is wider than innocent passage.
Hot pursuit. It must be continuous and it ends when the ship enters the territorial sea of its own or a third State. Candidates routinely omit the ending condition.
The transfer provision. Not transferring damage from one area to another, or transforming one type of pollution into another, is distinctive and quotable, and few candidates give it.

questions.understand_first: UNCLOS is often called the constitution of the oceans, and the description is exact: it does not regulate the detail of anything, it allocates AUTHORITY. Limb (b) is the heart of it - as you move seaward from the coast, the coastal State's power weakens by stages, from full sovereignty in the territorial sea, through specific enforcement powers in the contiguous zone, to resource rights only in the EEZ and on the shelf, to no sovereignty at all on the high seas. Learn it as one continuous gradient and the five zones stop being five separate definitions to memorise. Limb (a) then follows the same logic: UNCLOS states the duty to protect the marine environment and says who must set the rules and who may enforce them - but for ships it hands the actual technical standard-setting to the IMO. That is precisely why MARPOL exists and why UNCLOS itself contains no discharge limits.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs of eight marks. (a) asks for the important HIGHLIGHTS of UNCLOS on protection and preservation of the marine environment - a structured survey of Part XII, not a recital of article numbers. (b) asks for a brief explanation of five named zones, which is a definition-and-limits exercise where the distances and the rights in each zone are the marks.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 8 + 8 = 16. Limb (b) is five zones in eight marks - roughly a mark and a half each - so each needs limit, legal character and the key right, and nothing more. Limb (a) at eight marks needs several distinct highlights rather than one long paragraph on the general obligation, so it is organised into general duty, source-by-source coverage, enforcement, and the supporting machinery.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For (a): the general obligation to protect and preserve; that the sovereign right to exploit is qualified by it; the duty not to transfer damage from one area or type to another; that UNCLOS covers ALL sources of pollution, not just ships; that for vessel pollution it defers to the competent international organization, meaning IMO; and the three-way enforcement structure of flag, port and coastal State. For (b): the correct distances - 12, 24, 200 - measured from baselines, and the different legal quality of each zone.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: UNCLOS 1982 itself - Part II for the territorial sea and contiguous zone, Part V for the EEZ, Part VI for the continental shelf, Part VII for the high seas, and Part XII, articles 192 to 237, for the marine environment. The BBNJ Agreement is checked for status at the sitting date only and nothing is asserted from its content.

MEDIUM for one adjacent item: the BBNJ Agreement was ADOPTED on 19 June 2023, before this sitting, but did not enter into force until 17 January 2026, long after it. It may be mentioned as adopted and awaiting entry into force; it must never be written as applying.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The question is wholly international. India ratified UNCLOS, but the question asks nothing about Indian implementing legislation and nothing is asserted about the Maritime Zones Act or any other domestic statute.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: The continental shelf definition is the one genuinely difficult item, because it has both a distance limb and a geological limb and two alternative outer constraints. It is stated carefully. Baselines are explained once at the start of limb (b) because all five zones are measured from them and candidates routinely measure from the coastline instead.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the general environmental obligation under UNCLOS, and how is the right to exploit resources qualified?
retrieval_cards.answer: States have a general obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment. They have the sovereign right to exploit their natural resources pursuant to their own environmental policies, but in accordance with that duty. They must take all measures necessary to prevent, reduce and control pollution from any source, and must not transfer damage or hazards from one area to another or transform one type of pollution into another.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which sources of pollution does UNCLOS Part XII address?
retrieval_cards.answer: Land-based sources; seabed activities subject to national jurisdiction; activities in the Area; dumping; pollution from vessels; and pollution from or through the atmosphere. It is far wider than a shipping instrument, and land-based sources contribute the greater part of marine pollution.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does UNCLOS contain no discharge standards for ships?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because for vessel-source pollution it directs States to act through the competent international organization - the IMO - to establish international rules and standards, with national laws required to have at least the same effect. UNCLOS allocates the authority; the IMO instruments such as MARPOL supply the technical content.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who may enforce against pollution from ships under UNCLOS?
retrieval_cards.answer: The flag State, in respect of its own ships wherever the violation occurred; the port State, which may investigate and institute proceedings for a discharge even where it occurred outside its own waters; and the coastal State, for violations within its territorial sea or exclusive economic zone, with powers graduated by the seriousness of the harm.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the limits of the territorial sea, contiguous zone and EEZ, and from where they are measured.
retrieval_cards.answer: Territorial sea up to 12 nautical miles, contiguous zone up to 24 nautical miles, and exclusive economic zone up to 200 nautical miles - all measured from the baseline, normally the low-water line along the coast, not from the outer edge of the preceding zone.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish sovereignty in the territorial sea from sovereign rights in the EEZ.
retrieval_cards.answer: In the territorial sea the coastal State has full sovereignty, extending to the airspace above and the seabed and subsoil below, qualified only by the right of innocent passage. In the EEZ it has sovereign rights, not sovereignty - resource rights over the living and non-living resources, plus jurisdiction over artificial islands, marine scientific research and protection of the environment - while other States retain the freedoms of navigation, overflight and submarine cables.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the four matters over which the contiguous zone confers control?
retrieval_cards.answer: Customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary laws and regulations - CFIS. The coastal State may exercise the control necessary to prevent infringement of these within its territory or territorial sea, and to punish such infringement already committed there. It confers no general policing power and no sovereignty.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is the continental shelf defined, and what is distinctive about the rights over it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The seabed and subsoil beyond the territorial sea, throughout the natural prolongation of the land territory to the outer edge of the continental margin, or to 200 nautical miles where the margin does not extend that far - with outer limits constrained to 350 nautical miles or 100 nautical miles from the 2,500 metre isobath. The sovereign rights to explore and exploit its natural resources are exclusive and exist automatically, without occupation or proclamation, and do not affect the legal status of the waters or airspace above.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the high seas, and what are the exceptions to flag State jurisdiction there?
retrieval_cards.answer: All parts of the sea not included in the EEZ, territorial sea, internal waters or archipelagic waters. They are open to all States, reserved for peaceful purposes, and no State may subject any part to its sovereignty. Jurisdiction is with the flag State, subject to piracy, which any State may act against; the right of visit on reasonable suspicion of piracy, slave trading, unauthorised broadcasting or statelessness; and hot pursuit, which must be continuous and ends when the ship enters the territorial sea of its own or a third State.
